title: How we rebuilt the Shopify app in 12 weeks (2026)
summary: How we rebuilt the Shopify app in 12 weeks (2026) - Shopify Skip to Content blog | Mobile How we rebuilt the Shopify app in 12 weeks What changed when agents started writing our mobile code, and how we redesigned our architecture, tooling, and workflow around validation. by Remi ...
clean_content: How we rebuilt the Shopify app in 12 weeks (2026) - Shopify Skip to Content blog | Mobile How we rebuilt the Shopify app in 12 weeks What changed when agents started writing our mobile code, and how we redesigned our architecture, tooling, and workflow around validation. by Remi Vanhee Published on Nov 10, 2026 Thirty engineers just rebuilt the Shopify app from React Native to Swift and Kotlin in 12 weeks. The app has more than 300 screens, home and lockscreen widgets, an Apple Watch app, complications, and Siri Shortcuts. Agents wrote most of the code. If you have read our other posts in this series, that won’t be a surprise. The real surprising part is how much we had to change around the code. Once agents started producing large amounts of code quickly, everything surrounding that code became more important: the architecture, tests, code review process, machines running emulators, and coordination between people. We changed the way the app is built so agents could work inside a workflow with fast feedback, clear patterns, and checks that kept them on the rails. The posts we’ve shared over the last few weeks covered the main pieces of that system: Native is now the future of mobile at Shopify Helix, the internal tool powering our migration Our remote development environment for agents Reflex: an architecture for building mobile apps with agents This is about how those pieces fit together, and what we learned about setting up a workflow where agents can move fast while humans still validate, review, and approve what ships. How we prepared the app for agents Before we migrated screens, a small group of engineers prepared the system around the agents: the architecture, tooling, and the feedback loop. At first glance, that can look backwards. If an agent can generate thousands of lines of code in an afternoon, why spend weeks beforehand writing the screens? Because speed on its own gets you a lot of code, not a good app. The system around the agent has to tell it when the output is wrong, and the architecture has to steer it toward code that is clean, consistent, and performant. Left alone, agents won’t do that. The work was not just architecture in the usual sense. We were completely rethinking how mobile apps should be built in the age of AI agents: Business logic that runs without a device for fast feedback loops The Reflex architecture and a CLI that can load any screen in milliseconds One architecture shared by iOS and Android Clear examples and .md files for every new screen to follow Repository guardrails that fail when the code drifts For humans, architecture can live partly in people's heads. For agents, it cannot. It has to be visible in file structure, architecture.md files, skills, naming, state shapes, method signatures, CLI output, lint rules, test fixtures, and CI failures. That changed how we built the app. We were still designing for engineers, but we were also designing for agents that need repeatable patterns, fast feedback, and very clear error messages. Before this work, an agent had the same feedback loop as a human: build the app, start the emulator or simulator, navigate to the screen, look at the result by taking screenshots, analyze it, make a change, and try again. That loop takes several minutes per iteration, and agents are bad at every step that depends on visual navigation and context that lives outside the code. After the architecture work, an agent could run most of the screen without starting a device. It could load a ViewModel from the terminal, trigger actions, inspect state, and run deterministic checks in milliseconds. That fast feedback loop is what made the migration possible at the speed we reached later. We didn’t get faster by asking agents to take bigger swings. We got faster by making the work smaller and the feedback loop tighter. How we organized the actual rewrite About 30 engineers worked on the rewrite, organized in pods of two, with each pair owning an area of the app across both platforms. The two engineers in a pod paired most of the day, each one steering multiple agents at the same time. Agents kept working overnight and on weekends, so every morning started with a queue of PRs to review. We kept the pods small on purpose. Agents gave each pair the implementation capacity to cover a whole product area. What each pod needed was clear ownership, fast decisions, and shared context. We didn’t organize the migration as one iOS team and one Android team. Each pair owned a product area end to end. Agents did much of the implementation, but humans still owned the architecture, product behavior, and final judgment about what was good to ship. Consistency over platform-specific architecture Our first principle was consistency . Consistency of architecture, so agents could create PRs that followed the same shape. Consistency between Android and iOS, so the same screen exposed the same state, actions, and behavior on both platforms. An iOS ViewModel for the orders screen looks like the Android ViewModel, whether you’re reading the Swift or Kotlin version. We deliberately prioritized consistency over platform-specific architecture. Some of the code is less idiomatic than what an iOS or Android purist might write. We are comfortable with that tradeoff because of what we get in return: Every migrated screen becomes an example for the next one One PR contains the changes for both platforms An engineer who knows one platform can review a PR on the other Architecture guidelines are written once for both platforms Tests can run the same merchant journey across iOS and Android This is also what makes the argument from our first post work in practice. Building native apps for two platforms doesn’t have to cost twice as much if the second platform follows the same architecture. That only works if both sides keep the same shape. In an agentic workflow, consistency is not aesthetic. It’s infrastructure. It’s what lets humans compare intent across platforms, agents to reuse examples, and CI to detect drift before a reviewer has to find it by hand. We enforce that consistency. CI fails when iOS and Android diverge in ways the architecture doesn’t allow. Keeping agents on the rails TL;DR: No vibe coding. In our first post , we wrote that asking an LLM to one-shot a rewrite produces a huge amount of code that can’t be shipped. Guardrails are our answer to that problem. With a strong architecture and the right checks, agents have clear directions and less room to improvise in places where improvisation creates maintenance cost. Without those constraints, an agent can produce code that compiles, passes a narrow test, and still leaves humans with a codebase nobody wants to own. The system has to answer three questions for every agent-written change: Does it follow the architecture? Does it behave like the existing app? Can a human review the intent without reading a giant diff line by line? Different parts of the system answer those questions. The architecture guidelines, examples, lint rules, and divergence checks answer the first one. Helix and the legacy React Native app answer the second one. Small checkpoints, cross-platform PRs, and agent-first review answer the third. The important thing is that the guardrails live in the workflow, not only in a document. A document explains why the rule exists; CI decides whether the rule was followed. Agents need more than instructions. They need a way to discover when they are wrong. The existing app was the spec We tried spec-driven development first: write a spec for a screen, give it to the agent, review the result. It didn’t work. The specs went out of date almost immediately. By the time the agent was working on the third checkpoint of a screen, the spec written for the first checkpoint was already incomplete or wrong. Nobody wanted to maintain a parallel description of behavior that already existed in the product. For this migration, the existing app was a better spec than a do

title: Introducing CFSSL - CloudFlare's PKI toolkit
summary: Introducing CFSSL - CloudFlare's PKI toolkit | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content Today we’re proud to introduce CFSSL—our open source toolkit for everything TLS/SSL. CFSSL is used internally by CloudFlare for bundling TLS/SSL certificates chains, and for our internal Certificat...
clean_content: Introducing CFSSL - CloudFlare's PKI toolkit | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content Today we’re proud to introduce CFSSL—our open source toolkit for everything TLS/SSL. CFSSL is used internally by CloudFlare for bundling TLS/SSL certificates chains, and for our internal Certificate Authority infrastructure. We use this tool for all our TLS certificates. Creating a certificate bundle is a common pain point for website operators, and doing it right is important for website security AND speed (CloudFlare does both). Getting the correct bundle together is a black art, and can quickly become a debugging nightmare if it's not done correctly. We wrote CFSSL to make bundling easier. By picking the right chain of certificates, CFSSL solves the balancing act between performance, security, and compatibility. Staying true to our promise to make the web fast and safe, we’re open sourcing CFSSL. We believe CFSSL will be useful for anyone building a site using HTTPS—from website owners to large software-as-a-service companies. CFSSL is written in Go and available on the CloudFlare Github account . It can be used as a web service with a JSON API, and as a handy command line tool. CFSSL is the result of real-world expertise about how the TLS ecosystem on the Web works that you can gain by working at CloudFlare’s scale. These are hard-won lessons, applied in code. The rest of this blog post serves as an under-the-hood look at how and why CFSSL works, and how you can use it as a certificate bundler or as a lightweight CA. As you can see in the above image, the key is owned by CloudFlare, Inc., and the issuer is GlobalSign (a well-known CA). GlobalSign has issued a certificate named “GlobalSign Extended Validation CA - SHA256 - G2”; this G2 certificate is signed by another certificate called “GlobalSign Root CA - R2”. Note that the root certificate does not have an issuer—it is signed by its own private key. In other words, the root vouches for itself. The reason your browser trusts a root certificate is because browsers have a list of root certificates that they implicitly trust, and when a site is trusted it will show the lock icon to the left of the web address (see image below). Certain certificates are on the list typically because they have been around for some time, and they belong to certificate authorities that have gone through a rigorous security audit. GlobalSign is one of these trusted authorities; therefore, its root certificate is in the list of trusted root certificates for nearly every browser. What Are SSL Certificates? SSL certificates form the core of trust on the web by assuring the identity of websites. This trust is built by digitally binding a cryptographic key to an organization’s identity. An SSL certificate will bind domain names to server names, and company names to locations. This ensures that if you go to your bank’s web site, for example, you know for sure it is your bank, and you are not giving out your information to a phishing scam. A certificate is a file that contains a public key which is bound to a record of its owner. The mechanism that makes this binding trustworthy is called the Public Key Infrastructure and public-key cryptography is the glue that makes this possible. A certificate is associated with a private key that corresponds to the certificate's public key, which is stored separately. The certificate comes with a digital signature from a trusted third-party called a certificate authority or CA. Let's examine the cloudflare.com certificate. The length of intermediate certificates in a chain can vary, but chains will always have one leaf and one root. Unfortunately, there is a catch for the owner of the leaf certificate: presenting only the leaf certificate to the browser is usually not enough. The intermediate certificates are not always known to the browser, requiring the website to include them with the leaf certificate. The list of certificates that the browser needs to validate a certificate is called a certificate bundle. It should contain all the certificates in the chain up to the first certificate known to the browser. In the case of the CloudFlare website, this bundle contains both the cloudflare.com certificate and the GlobalSign G2 intermediate. CFSSL was written to make certificate bundling easier. How CFSSL Makes Certificate Bundling Easier If you are running a website (or perhaps some other TLS-based service) and need to install a certificate, CFSSL can create the certificate bundle for you. Start with the following command: $ cfssl bundle -cert mycert.crt This will output a JSON blob containing the chain of certificates along with relevant information extracted from that chain. Alternatively, you can run the CFSSL service that responds to requests with a JSON API: $ cfssl serve This command opens up an HTTP service on localhost that accepts requests. To bundle using this API, send a POST request to this service, [http://localhost:8888/api/v1/cfssl/bundle](http://localhost:8888/api/v1/cfssl/bundle) , using a JSON request such as: { "certificate": } CloudFlare’s SSL service will return a JSON response of the form: { "result": {}, "success": true, "errors": [], "messages": [], } (Developers take note: this response format is a preview of our upcoming CloudFlare API rewrite; with this API, we can use CFSSL as a service for certificate bundling and more—stay tuned.) If you upload your certificate to CloudFlare, this is what is used to create a certificate bundle for your website. To create a certificate bundle with CFSSL, you need to know which certificates are trusted by the browsers you hope to display content to. In a controlled corporate environment, this is usually easy since every browser is set up with the same configuration; however, it becomes more difficult when creating a bundle for the web. Different Certs for Different Folks Each browser has unique capabilities and configurations, and a certificate bundle that’s trusted in one browser might not be trusted in another; this can happen for several reasons: Different browsers trust different root certificates. Some browsers trust more root certificates than others. For example, the NSS root store used in Firefox trusts 143 certificates; however, Windows 8.1 trusts 391 certificates. So a bundle with a chain that expects the browser to trust a certificate exclusive to the Windows root store will appear as untrusted in Firefox. Older systems might have old root stores. Some browsers run on older systems that have not been updated to trust recently-created certificate authorities. For example, Android 2.2 and earlier don't trust the “GoDaddy Root Certificate Authority G2” because that root certificate was created after they were released. Older systems don't support modern cryptography. Users on Windows XP SP2 and earlier can't validate certificates signed by certain intermediates. This includes the “DigiCert SHA2 High Assurance Server CA” because the hash function SHA-2 used in this certificate was standardised after Windows XP was released. In order to provide maximum compatibility between SSL chains and browsers, you often have to pick a different certificate chain than the one originally provided to you by your CA. This alternate chain might contain a different set of intermediates that are signed by a different root certificate. Alternate chains can be troublesome. They tend to contain a longer list of certificates than the default chain from the CA, and longer chains cause site connections to be slower. This lag is because the web server needs to send more certificates (i.e. more data) to the browser, and the browser has to spend time verifying more certificates on its end. Picking the right chain can be tricky. CFSSL helps pick the right certificate chain, selecting for performance, security, and compatibility. summary: Componentizing Shopify’s Tax Engine - Shopify Skip to Content blog | Development Componentizing Shopify’s Tax Engine How Shopify built for the long term by moving our tax engine to a componentized architecture within Shopify’s codebase with zero downtime. by Chris Inch Published ...
clean_content: Componentizing Shopify’s Tax Engine - Shopify Skip to Content blog | Development Componentizing Shopify’s Tax Engine How Shopify built for the long term by moving our tax engine to a componentized architecture within Shopify’s codebase with zero downtime. by Chris Inch Published on Jul 5, 2019 By Chris Inch and Vignesh Sivasubramanian Reading Time: 8 minutes At Shopify, we value building for the long term. This can come in many forms but within Engineering, we want to build things in a way that is easy to understand, modify, and deploy so we are confident to build without introducing bugs or unnecessary complexity. The tax engine that existed in Shopify’s codebase started out simple, but over years of development and incremental additions, it became a challenging part of code to work within. This article details how our Engineering team tackled the problems associated with complex code, and how we built for the long term by moving our tax engine to a componentized architecture within Shopify’s codebase. Oh… and we did all this without anyone noticing. Tax Calculations: The Wild West Tax calculations on orders are complex by nature. Many factors go into calculating the final amount charged in taxes on an order like product type, customer location, shipping origin, physical and economic nexus of a business. This complexity created a complicated system within our product where ownership of tax logic was spread far and wide to components that knew too much about how tax calculations worked. It felt like the Wild West of tax code. Lucky for us, we have a well-defined componentization architecture at Shopify  and we leveraged this architecture to implement a new tax component. Essentially, we needed to retain the complexity, but eliminate the complications. Here’s how we did it. Educate the Team The first step to making things less complicated was creating a team that would spend time gaining knowledge of the code base around tax. We needed to fully understand which parts of Shopify were influencing tax calculations and how they were being used. And it’s not just code! Taxes are tricky in general. To be able to create a tax component, one must not only understand the code involved, but also understand the tax domain itself. We used an in-house tax Subject Matter Expert (SME) to ensure we continued to support the many complexities of calculating taxes. We also employed different strategies to bring the team’s tax knowledge up to snuff which included weekly trivia question on taxes around the world. This allowed us to learn the domain and have a bit of fun while doing so. Do you know the difference between zero-rated taxes and no taxes? No? Neither did we but with persistence and a tenacity for learning, the team leveled up with all the intricacies of taxation faced by Shopify merchants. We realized if we wanted to make taxes an independent component in our system, we need to be able to discern what proper tax calculations look like. Understand Existing Tax Logic The team figured out where tax logic was used by other systems and how it was consumed. This initial step took the most effort as we used a lot of regular expressions, scripts, and manual processes to find all of the areas that touched taxes. We found that the best way to gain expertise quickly was to work on any known bugs relating to taxes. There was some re-factoring that was beneficial to tackle up front, before componentization, but some of the tax logic was so intertwined with other systems that it would be easier to re-factor once the larger componentization change was in place. Taxes Before Componentization After a full understanding of the tax logic was achieved, the team devised the best strategy to isolate the tax logic into its own component. A component is an efficient way to organize large sections of code that changes together by breaking a large code base into meaningful distinct parts, each with its own defined dependencies. After this, all communication becomes explicit over the component’s architectural boundaries. For example, one of the most complicated aspects of Shopify’s code is order creation. During the creation of an order, the tax engine is invoked by three distinct parts of Shopify Cart -> Checkout -> Order. This change of context brings in more complexity to the system because each area is using taxes in its own selfish way, without consistency. When Checkout changed how it used Taxes , it might have unknowingly broken how Cart was using it. Creating a Tax Component Define the Interface In order to componentize the tax logic, first we had to define a clear interface and entry point into all the tax calls being made in Shopify’s codebase. Everything that requires tax information will pass a set of defined parameters, and expect a specific response when requesting tax rates. The tax request outlines the data it requires in a clear and understandable format. Each of the complex attributes is simply a collection of simple types, this way the tax logic need not worry about the implementation of the caller. The tax response schema is also composed of simple types that don't make any assumptions about the calling component. Componentized Tax Engine This above diagram shows how each component interacts cleanly with the tax engine using well-defined requests and responses, TaxesRequestSchema and TaxesReponseSchema . With the new interface, the flow of execution on tax engine looks much more streamlined and easy to understand. Executing the Plan Once we had defined a clean interface to make tax requests, it was time to wrangle all the instances of tax-aware code throughout the entire Shopify codebase. We did this by moving all source files touching tax logic under tax component. If taxes were the Wild West, then we were the Sheriff coming to town. We couldn’t leave any rogue tax code outside of our tax component. Additionally, we wanted to make our changes future-proof so that other developers at Shopify aren’t able to accidentally add new code that reaches past our component boundaries, so we added GitHub bot triggers to notify our team on any commits pushed against source files under tax component, this allowed us to be sure that no additional dependencies were added to the system while it is undergoing change. Updating our Tax Testing Suites Every line of code that we moved within the component was tested and cleaned. Existing unit tests were re-checked, and new integrations tests were written. We added end-to-end scenarios for each consumer of the tax component until we were satisfied that it tested the usage of tax logic sufficiently— this was the best way to capture failures that may have been introduced to the system as a whole. The unit tests provided confidence that the individual units of our code produced the same functionality and our integration tests provided confidence that our new component did not alter the macro functionality of the system. Slowly but surely, we completed work on the tax component. Finally, it was ready, and there was just one thing left to do: start using it. Releasing Our code cleanup work was complete, and the only task left was releasing it. We had high confidence in the changes we introduced through componentization of this logic. Even still, we needed to ensure we did not change the behavior of the existing system for the hundreds of thousands of merchants who rely on tax calculations within Shopify while we released it. Up to this point, the code paths into the component were not yet being used in production. For our team, it was paramount that the overall calculation of taxes remained unaffected, so we took a systematic, methodological and measurable approach to releasing. The Experimental Code Path The first step to our release was to ensure that our shiny new component was calculating taxes the same way that our existing tax engine was already calculating these same taxes. We accomplished this by running an “expe

title: How Shopify turns open models into task experts (2026)
summary: How Shopify turns open models into task experts (2026) - Shopify Skip to Content blog | AI & Machine Learning How Shopify turns open models into task experts Sidekick’s frontier model hands its most token-heavy work to open models that Shopify post-trains and serves itself. H...
clean_content: How Shopify turns open models into task experts (2026) - Shopify Skip to Content blog | AI & Machine Learning How Shopify turns open models into task experts Sidekick’s frontier model hands its most token-heavy work to open models that Shopify post-trains and serves itself. Here’s the loop we use to build them, and where NVIDIA’s models, software, and GPUs make each turn faster and cheaper. by Andrew McNamara / Logan Vegna Published on Oct 21, 2026 Sidekick , Shopify’s AI commerce assistant, runs on a frontier model that talks to the merchant, plans the work, and calls tools. For focused jobs, it hands off work to subagents, several of which run open models we’ve post-trained for that one task. Take the GraphQL subagent. When a merchant asks, “Which products are almost out of stock?”, it reads Shopify’s API schema, searches the docs, writes and runs a query, and returns the results. That work is context-heavy: the subagent reads about 40 tokens for every one it writes, and a frontier model’s API charges for every one of them. For that subagent, we built a task expert by post-training NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On this task, it scores slightly higher than the frontier model, responds 7× faster, and costs about 90% less to serve. And because Shopify controls the post-trained weights, we can serve the model on our own GPUs and decide when it changes. The loop that builds them is Sidekick’s continual learning loop, with a hardware twist. The Model Optimization Flywheel. Three setup steps define the target, and the loop then repeats with each new batch of production data. Green tags mark NVIDIA technology. Every task expert goes through the same steps: Define quality Product experts turn requirements into a scoring rubric. For GraphQL, it covers completeness, execution, and response quality. How closely two experts agree on the same conversations sets the bar, and we tune an LLM judge with the GEPA and ACE optimizers until it agrees with held-out human labels just as well. From then on, the judge scores every agent change, candidate model, and training run. Improve the frontier agent Before an open model enters the picture, we push the frontier-model version of the agent as far as it will go. An autoresearch loop proposes one small change at a time to the prompts, tool descriptions, or control flow, and keeps the change only if the judge’s score improves. The improved agent is the bar the open model has to beat. Choose an open model We don’t pretrain. We test open models like NVIDIA Nemotron inside the real subagent, with the same tools and judge, and weigh starting quality, serving speed, and support in NVIDIA Megatron Bridge, which we train with. For GraphQL, we chose Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a mixture-of-experts model with three billion of its 30 billion parameters active per token. Optimize inference We measure serving from the start, because a model that’s too slow for production isn’t worth post-training. We benchmark every workload with NVIDIA AIPerf, an open-source  load tester in NVIDIA Dynamo, which replays production traces with synthetic text instead of customer data. Shopify contributed support for live-response replay , so multi-turn tests hit the server’s prefix cache the way production does. Those measurements guide our choice of serving stack. For Buyer Profile, a batch job, AIPerf compared vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM. TensorRT-LLM did the most work per GPU. In NVIDIA’s measurements, SimGym (our shopping simulator) ran 4.5× faster on Blackwell B200 than on H200, at 1.48× lower cost. Turn failures into training data Self-healing turns a failed production conversation into a training example. Over 86 nightly runs, it repaired 69% of the failures it tried. Every night, the judge scores a sample of production GraphQL conversations, and anything short of perfect goes to self-healing. A frontier model acting as critic writes a hint, never the answer, and a simulated merchant reruns the request with it against the same store. If the judge passes the rerun, we remove the hint, anonymize the conversation, and add it to the training set. If not, the critic tries again, up to three times. Over 86 nightly runs recently, self-healing repaired 59,535 GraphQL conversations—69% of the failures it tried. Human annotators corrected the rest, and their corrections join the ground truth that calibrates the judge. Post-train on Blackwell We post-train with NVIDIA Megatron Bridge, which brings standard Hugging Face checkpoints onto NVIDIA’s Megatron Core training library without rewriting the model, and scales across nodes on Nebius by changing settings, not code. Blackwell makes each loop cheaper: on the same FP8 post-training job for our Analytics model, eight B300 GPUs trained 1.86× faster than eight H200s, using 46% fewer GPU-hours. Then the judge scores the new checkpoint, and the loop starts again. Hopper versus Blackwell on Shopify workloads. Training: the same FP8 post-training job for our Analytics model on eight GPUs. Serving: SimGym, in NVIDIA’s measurements. Results on GraphQL GraphQL judge score for Nemotron 3.5 Lightning across six flywheel loops, with the healed examples added in each loop. Out of the box, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning scored 37.7 on our GraphQL judge; the frontier model scored 73. The first loop took it to 61.5, and after six loops and 61,000 healed examples, the post-trained model scored 74.5. GraphQL load test, replaying production traffic with AIPerf: response time per request at the median and for the slowest 1% (p99), and serving cost compared with the frontier model. The post-trained model is also much faster. In an AIPerf replay of production GraphQL traffic, post-trained Nemotron returned a full response in 0.87 seconds at the median, against 6.50 seconds for the frontier model’s API, and its slowest 1% of requests finished 8× sooner. It also beat another post-trained open model of comparable size, which was close at the median but more than twice as slow at p99. Serving cost on that traffic is about 90% lower than the frontier model’s. Across our post-trained models, self-hosting cuts serving cost by 90-98% compared with frontier model pricing. Frontier intelligence, specialist efficiency The frontier model keeps the work it’s best at: talking to the merchant and deciding what to call. The token-heavy specialist work moves to open models we own, and every turn of the flywheel compounds: human corrections sharpen the judge, production traffic grows the training set, and each generation of NVIDIA hardware and software makes the next loop faster and cheaper to run. Thanks to NVIDIA's Megatron Bridge, AIPerf, TensorRT-LLM, and Nemotron teams; the CentML team (now part of NVIDIA); and Nebius. Adapted from our NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 talk. We’ll look at how to: view metrics in the EFS console use the CloudWatch console and API collect metrics with Linux tools collect EFS logs with AWS logging services and Linux logging tools Collect EFS metrics Collecting and analyzing EFS metrics can help you understand your file systems’ role in the health and performance of your applications. Because EFS is a managed service, some standard approaches to monitoring, such as monitoring server resource metrics, are not applicable. In this section, we’ll look at some tools provided by AWS and some that are built into Linux that let you collect and visualize key EFS metrics. The EFS console You can use the EFS console, which is available from within the AWS Management Console , to create and delete file systems, define their settings, and manage mount targets and access points. [&>.iframe-block-wrapper]:desktop-sm:col-span-8" data-astro-cid-twmmywjp> Developer experience, commonly known as DevEx, describes how an organization’s systems, workflows, tools, and culture affect developer productivity. A positive DevEx leads to tangible organizational benefits, including faster releases, increased innovation, and reduced technical debt. Measuring DevEx enables engineering management to quantify their team’s impact and understand where to direct improvement efforts. While there are differing approaches to DevEx measurement , attempting to quantify it in terms of individual metrics is always a temptation. The widespread use of AI has only added to that temptation, with leaders measuring individual token consumption in addition to metrics like lines of code or PR count. But tracking what is easy to count can adversely impact DevEx, and the gap between individual metrics and developer productivity continues to widen. According to the 2025 JetBrains Developer Ecosystem survey , 66% of developers do not believe that current metrics reflect their contributions. Atlassian’s 2025 State of Developer Experience report found that 63% of developers do not believe leaders understand their pain points, a sentiment that increased significantly from 44% in 2024. In this post, we’ll discuss how to avoid the five most common pitfalls that organizations fall into when measuring DevEx in the AI era: Measuring individual output instead of system health Relying on system metrics without perceptual data Equating AI adoption with efficiency Treating AI token usage as a productivity metric Measuring without developer buy-in Measuring individual output instead of system health Output metrics like lines of code, PR count, number of commits, and story points can provide valuable insight when analyzed at a team level, but undermine developer trust, incentivize gaming, and discourage collaboration when tracked at the individual level. Mentorship, code review, task planning, and knowledge sharing are all collaborative efforts that SPACE framework researchers have identified as “invisible” yet highly valuable work that benefits the entire organization. When individual output is tracked, developers may be incentivized to devote a disproportionate amount of time to the work that appears on a dashboard. Track system health to improve DevEx outcomes Goodhart’s law states, “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” For example, if you track the number of PRs per developer, they may split up commits to generate more PRs; if you track individual deployment frequency, they may deploy trivial changes. The metrics will improve without a parallel meaningful improvement in productivity. Datadog engineering leadership has made it clear that the goal of measurement is never to evaluate individual performance. title: Three years after World IPv6 Day
summary: Three years after World IPv6 Day | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content It’s been over 1,000 days since the Internet Society’s World IPv6 Day and a lot of positive things have happened in that world of IPv6 content delivery. At CloudFlare we have not been sitting still either. Providi...
clean_content: Three years after World IPv6 Day | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content It’s been over 1,000 days since the Internet Society’s World IPv6 Day and a lot of positive things have happened in that world of IPv6 content delivery. At CloudFlare we have not been sitting still either. Providing IPv6 access is core to our services and each and every customer has full IPv4 and IPv6 services available when their website is CloudFlare enabled. Starting three months ago CloudFlare moved to make IPv6 enabled the default setting for all new accounts and for existing accounts that had simply sat on the default settings mode. This resulted in an uptick in the IPv6 traffic stats from our network and was noticed globally . Our support issues have been near zero; which makes sense as the previous three years has been a fantastic proving ground for IPv6 networking. IPv6 is here today and it works. But it's still not widely used. It's time for that to change. 20% of the IPv6 web uses CloudFlare IPv6 Looking at the top one million web sites tracked by Alexa we see that around 7% are accessible using IPv6. Of that 7% a full 20% are accessible using IPv6 because they are CloudFlare customers with IPv6 enabled. We hope and expect that both those percentages will grow over time. The web logfile problem However some complex sites, that use the origin server IP address within their codebase, have had issues enabling IPv6. Many sites log the IP address of the visitor when a web page is accessed. This has caused some interesting headaches when migrating to IPv6. Why? Because when software developers hardcode a 4-byte IPv4-address into a database they will have a near-impossible time dealing with at 16-byteIPv6 address. Take a look at this IETF style graphic showing the overall size of the two addressing schemes. IPv4 (32 bits) +----+----+ |####|####| +----+----+ IPv6 (128 bits) +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+ |####|####|####|####|####|####|####|####| +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+ When a developer uses a string (or character) area to store the IP address there’s a string length issue. In IPv4, the maximum length could be represented by the IP address 255.255.255.255 (which is 15 bytes long). For IPv6 the address could be FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF (which is 39 bytes long). Some programming languages and databases can be string length agnostic; however most aren’t. Pseudo IPv4 to the (Temporary) Rescue As a stopgap measure CloudFlare has introduced a pseudo IPv4 address that is mapped from the real IPv6 address and can be used in place of the IPv6. It's not a perfect solution and software and databases are going to have to be upgraded to support IPv6, but in the meantime this pseudo IPv4 address can be used where an IPv4 format address is expected. Going forward This workaround is now available for every CloudFlare customer and we promise to persuade as many of our users who have chosen to disable IPv6 to enable IPv6 fully. Those few remaining sites will want to be part of the new Internet. Happy third anniversary World IPv6 Day! title: Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks | AWS Security Blog
summary: Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks | AWS Security Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Security Blog Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authe...
clean_content: Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks | AWS Security Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Security Blog Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM key, confirm the new selector is live, and verify that your DMARC policy is already set to p=reject. Days later, you see that the same unfamiliar traffic is still authenticating as you. In this post, you learn why rotation alone can’t stop a DKIM replay attack, how to confirm that you’re looking at a replay rather than a legitimate relay or ordinary spoofing, and the DNS cleanup step that most rotation guidance leaves out. You also learn how you can use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to detect and respond to this activity faster. How DKIM replay works DKIM verifies one thing: that specific parts of a message didn’t change between the signer and the receiver. The signer signs the message with a private key, and receivers fetch the matching public key from your domain’s DNS to check the signature. A valid signature continues to validate wherever the message travels afterward. Mailing lists, .forward rules, and third-party relays all preserve it, which is the protocol working as designed. A replay attack takes advantage of that durability. The attack works as follows: Your ecommerce platform sends a customer a legitimate response email, signed with your DKIM key. An attacker obtains one copy of that message. They might subscribe to your mailing list, compromise a mailbox, retrieve it from a list archive, or capture it through a forwarding rule. The attacker resends that message, unchanged, from their own servers to thousands of new recipients. Each receiving server fetches your public key from DNS and checks the signature. The signature passes, because the body wasn’t modified. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) fails, because the sending IP isn’t yours, but DMARC requires only one of SPF or DKIM to pass with alignment. Because DKIM passes, DMARC passes, and the message is delivered as authenticated email from your domain. Understanding what an attacker can and can’t do matters, because the limits define the problem. An attacker can’t modify your message, add new content, or read your email. The signature is only valid while the message remains byte-for-byte identical. What an attacker gains is your domain’s reputation, which they use to deliver your genuine message to an audience you didn’t intend. A receipt or invoice becomes a lure, and email that would normally be filtered is delivered because receivers trust your domain. This is abuse of reputation and reach, not content forgery, and the distinction matters when you explain the incident to your security team. This also explains why an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t stop an attack. DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes with alignment. During a replay, DKIM passes, so DMARC passes, and p=reject does not apply. A p=reject policy is designed to stop spoofing, where a forger has no valid signature and DKIM fails. It does nothing against a message that you signed. Determining which of the two was used is what tells you how to respond. Is it replay, spoofing, or a legitimate relay? Email from an unfamiliar IP address that passes DKIM has three common explanations, and each requires a different response. Confirm which you’re dealing with before you make any changes. DMARC aggregate (rua) reports provide the source IP address, message volume, and SPF and DKIM results. This is enough to identify an anomaly, but not to prove a replay. A report row might read as follows: source IP: 203.0.113.45 | count: 4,200 | SPF: fail | DKIM: pass (d=yourdomain.com) You need to evaluate that row against the three possibilities: The first possibility is a legitimate relay that you haven’t inventoried, such as a mailing list, a forwarder, or an email security gateway such as an inline cloud access security broker (CASB) that you route through. The signature validly survives the relay, and this is normal email flow. In the report, the source IP address usually resolves to a known provider, and the volume tracks your actual sending. The second possibility is replay abuse, in which an attacker redistributes a message that you legitimately signed. In this case, the DKIM-passing volume comes from an IP address that has no business relationship with you, often well above the usual number of recipients that you send to, and frequently to recipient domains that you haven’t worked with. The third possibility is ordinary spoofing, which is a forgery with no valid signature. That row shows DKIM: fail. DKIM that passes from an unknown IP address is therefore usually not ordinary spoofing. Aggregate counts can’t prove a replay on their own. To confirm a replay, you need message-level evidence: a specific message that you sent matched to one that reached recipients you didn’t address. If you can’t make that match, treat the activity as an unconfirmed anomaly, and begin with the enforcement and monitoring steps that follow rather than removing keys. Set up an enforcing DMARC policy first Before you take any other action, confirm that you’re enforcing DMARC. Many domains that encounter this problem are still at p=none, which is monitoring only. This situation is common. Every DMARC deployment begins at p=none, and many organizations do not advance beyond it because nothing appears to be broken. At p=none, receivers take no action on failures, so no change you make affects delivery, and you can’t determine what enforcement would have caught. The first step is therefore not key removal; it’s completing your sender inventory and reaching enforcement: Inventory every legitimate sender and relay for your domain, including your email service providers, mailing lists, and any security gateways that send on your behalf. Bring each sender into SPF and DKIM alignment so that legitimate email authenticates. Advance the policy one stage at a time, from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. Review your rua reports at each stage before you advance, typically for a week or two per stage, and longer if you have many senders to work through. The pct tag lets you ramp up gradually, for example by quarantining 25% of failing email before you increase the percentage. After you’re enforcing DMARC, receivers that honor DMARC drop unauthenticated spoofing on your behalf. Only after this baseline is in place, and only after you have confirmed a replay of genuinely signed email, does the next step apply. Remove the old key from DNS: routine hygiene after rotation Most rotation guidance omits this step. Rotating a key and removing the old key are two separate actions. Rotation means that your provider begins signing new email with a new key and selector. Removal means deleting the old public key from DNS, so that previously signed messages, including the copies that an attacker captured, can no longer be verified. If you rotate but leave the old public key published, every message ever signed with that key remains replayable for as long as the record exists. Removing the old key is what closes that window and is the step that’s commonly overlooked. Removal affects only messages that are still in transit and were signed with the old key. After email is delivered, the receiver no longer needs your key, so we recommend that you leave the old key published long enough for in-flight email to arrive and then remove it. How much of this process you manage yourself depends on your DKIM method, which the following section describes. During a confirmed active replay, closing this window is essential. How you manage ke

title: Transit and Peering: How your requests reach GitHub - The GitHub Blog
summary: Transit and Peering: How your requests reach GitHub - The GitHub Blog Ross McFarland · @ross October 12, 2017 | 6 minutes Share: GitHub is at a scale that provides exposure to interesting aspects of running a major site and are working to mature and level-up many parts of our inf...
clean_content: Transit and Peering: How your requests reach GitHub - The GitHub Blog Ross McFarland · @ross October 12, 2017 | 6 minutes Share: GitHub is at a scale that provides exposure to interesting aspects of running a major site and are working to mature and level-up many parts of our infrastructure as we grow. One of the areas where this is evident is in how your requests find their destination using DNS and make their way into our sites over transit and peering. Many organizations are either too small to need to tackle these sorts of problems or so large they have groups to maintain existing solutions for each portion of them. It is really compelling to be able to directly work on such projects and closely with great engineers who are solving others still. Network Ingress The foundation is built with links to Internet providers referred to as transit . Conceptually they’re similar to the connection you have at home, a link through which you can reach any other point on the Internet. The biggest difference is that IP blocks can be announced as reachable through the link via BGP . Like your home connection the link will have an IP address, but in contrast that IP address is an implementation detail and not directly used by us to serve github.com . We instead announce blocks of IP addresses, for example 192.30.253.0/24 . When an ISP sees packets with a destination address in that range, they will forward them towards the best source of the announcement. Another difference is how transit is priced, typically billed by bandwidth in Mbps, megabit per second, at the 95th percentile . We have multiple providers in each of our regions with diverse links spread across routers. These links are commonly referred to as cross-connects and are physical strands of fiber optic cable that run from our device to theirs within the same facility. In early 2015, 100% of our requests arrived over transit links directly into our IAD data center. In the past two and a half years we’ve grown that substantially, now landing over double that capacity at each our IAD and SEA edge sites. As part of that move we’ve gained access to high quality peering . Broadly speaking peering is a connection established directly between two networks. The main difference between peering and transit is that peering only allows you to reach things on the peer’s network. You generally can’t “transit” them to reach others. We have two types of peering currently in use. The first is private network interconnect (PNI), a direct connection between their routers and ours. This is generally used when a sufficiently large volume of traffic regularly travels between the two networks. For us it can consist of a single pair of 10Gbps links or many pairs as required by the bandwidth and availability needs. The other type of peering we do is over Internet exchanges . In the case of exchange based peering instead of direct connections between the two networks’ routers, a connection is made through an intermediate network specifically for connecting peers. Through the exchange hundreds of other networks can get access to us and vice versa. Since there’s no per-peer physical resources being used beyond the initial exchange connection it’s effectively free to peer in this way and in fact exchange based peering is commonly settlement free, meaning no money changes hands. This is often the case for PNI as well. While peering can cut costs, that’s often a secondary benefit. The real upsides are in performance and availability. Having a direct connection means that traffic between the two networks is 100% in the control of two parties who are able to communicate with each other. It also means fewer hops between the source and destination which can improve latency considerably and avoid congestion. The increases in our transit capacity, addition of a second region, and the work on GLB , our load-balancing tier, has allowed us to handle volumetric DDoS attacks that in the past would have impacted our users. We’re very proud of that progress and always working to improve it further. Traffic Engineering The first step in the process of contacting GitHub is to direct things to the closest region. We use DNS , specifically GeoDNS to return a record based on the geographic location of the IP address doing the lookup. We conduct network level measurements using tools like RIPE Atlas and instrument our applications to collect similar information on real user requests. This data allows us to make choices on which locations should be serviced in SEA and which are best sent to IAD. We configure our split authority DNS providers with the results. Now that your request has a destination, network routing takes over. There are dozens of last hops your requests can take into our sites and nearly boundless options for getting to that point. To take a seemingly intractable problem and solve it millions of times per second at each point in the network, things have to be simplified. This is accomplished by localizing decisions. Each hop along the path between yours and our network makes its own choice using an algorithm like BGP route selection . This allows an extremely quick next hop decision to be made for a packet. There are a number of inputs into the process, but conceptually each device has its own idea of the best link to send a packet down in order to get it closer to its ultimate destination. We have the ability to influence the decisions by withdrawing or modifying our announcements, but ultimately control rests with the network devices and operators who set local preferences based on costs, capacity, health, and other factors. The adjustments we make are most often in response to large incidents with our direct or indirect providers, and aim to shift the traffic away from a specific trouble spot or temporarily remove a provider altogether. It’s important to note that at this level there’s no fundamental difference between transit and peering. Both use the same mechanisms to make next hop decisions, it’s that the best next hop when peered directly with someone is almost certainly over that connection when things are operating normally. Take away that link and the algorithm would fall back to its next best option, likely a transit link. Current State To recap, we have two major types of connectivity – transit and peering. Within peering, we have two sub-types, PNI and IX. We’ve talked previously about our internal network metrics and we have the same types of data for our points of ingress/egress. The image above shows our ingress and egress traffic for the past week across transit, PNI, and Exchange links. Especially interesting is that peering accounts for 60-70% of our traffic. That’s a huge deal, it means that three quarters of our bandwidth has an optimal path between its origin and destination, providing best case performance and cost savings for both parties. If you happen to have an exchange connected network check out our PeeringDB page and reach out if you’re interested in connecting. If you’re excited about network and traffic engineering, we’re looking to add Site Reliability Engineers and an Engineering Manager to the team. title: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI | AWS Security Blog
summary: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI | AWS Security Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Security Blog Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials g...
clean_content: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI | AWS Security Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Security Blog Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere , now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) . IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption. In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation. Note : As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments. X.509 certificates for workload identity If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes. As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs . In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA) . To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes. Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services Temporary access credentials Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor. To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session. Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information. Create a trust anchor. Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload. Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles. Trust model The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor . The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA. Certificate attributes Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation. The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl . -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE MQswC ........... -----END CERTIFICATE---- Certificate: Data: Version: 3 (0x2) Serial Number: e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3 Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA Validity Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (384 bit) pub: 04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05: X509v3 extensions: X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical CA:FALSE X509v3 Key Usage: critical Digital Signature Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66: IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation. "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" Note : An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere. Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession . To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": [ "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID" ] } } } ] } As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown

title: Update: More Page View Counting Refinement
summary: Update: More Page View Counting Refinement | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content We've written about the challenge of classifying what is a "page view" a couple times before (see Understanding Analytics: When Is a Page View Not a Page View? and A Quick Update on Page Vi...
clean_content: Update: More Page View Counting Refinement | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content We've written about the challenge of classifying what is a "page view" a couple times before (see Understanding Analytics: When Is a Page View Not a Page View? and A Quick Update on Page Views ). CloudFlare sees all web traffic so we're able to more accurately report on numbers like Unique IPs and Hits than other analytics systems like Google Analytics that use beacon-based tracking. Beacon-Based vs. Hits Tracking Google Analytics will only see the visitors that trigger their Javascript beacon, so they can't report on crawlers and bots that don't fire the request. Google Analytics also only sees the views of the pages where the beacon is fired, which means if you're trying to get an operations number like the number of requests per second your server is handling you have to estimate it rather than knowing it precisely. CloudFlare has the opposite challenge. We see every request from every visitor to your site. As a result, our hits number is not an estimation but an exact count. Similarly, our Uniques number is precise, deduped count of the number of unique IP addresses that visited your site. With CloudFlare, you don't need to trigger Javascript to be counted, so we end up counting a lot of traffic beacon-based analytics systems miss. That's not to say Google Analytics and other beacon-based tracking is bad. There's a place for both. If you're trying to see how many ads you serve, which is Google's primary interest, then it's good to use a tracking method that is the same as how ad tags are triggered. Therefore, beacon-based tracking makes sense. If you're trying to understand the total load on your server and other operations issues, which is CloudFlare's primary interest, then it make sense to count total requests. What Hits Are Page Views? Our challenge is that we then have to look at all the "hits" we see and classify which one of those actually counts as a page view. We're constantly making refinements to the algorithm that make it more accurate. We just pushed out a change to this algorithm late last week. It fixes some cases where objects were reporting their content type as text/html when they were actually images or non-HTML that shouldn't be counted as page views. It also fixes instances where we were counting some 300 redirects as page views, which effectively caused double counting of page views in some cases. The net impact on overall page view stats for most sites is very small (less than 1%). However, for some sites they'll see a more significant drop (as much as 20%). The change will impact analytics data going forward beginning last Thursday. Unfortunately, we don't store the raw historical data so it's not possible for us to update past analytics reports. The cases where there is a larger drop align with sites that previously reported a high deviation between our page view numbers and those numbers reported from Google Analytics. Now the two page view stats should be closer in line with one another, although CloudFlare still should report a higher number because we're picking up page views from crawlers and other visitors that don't trigger Javascript. As you'd expect, there's no change to the uniques or hits numbers since those are much more straight forward for us to count and report. We'll continue to refine all our analytics systems to report data about your as accurately as possible. title: How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions | AWS Architecture Blog
summary: How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions | AWS Architecture Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Architecture Blog How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions Every day, Zillow sends home shoppers more than 100 million personalized ...
clean_content: How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions | AWS Architecture Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Architecture Blog How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions Every day, Zillow sends home shoppers more than 100 million personalized email and push notifications: saved search alerts, home recommendations, property updates, seller reports, and reminders. These messages are one of Zillow’s core ways to engage home shoppers, and Zillow delivers them on time with consistent behavior across every campaign. Today, each of those notifications runs as its own short-lived workflow execution on AWS Step Functions Express Workflows. The underlying shape of this work isn’t unique to real estate. Many systems run the same kind of workflow at high volume: take an event, enrich it from several services, apply rules, assemble an output, and send it. This post shows how Zillow built one configuration-driven orchestration system to run that pattern at scale, and what teams across many domains can reuse from it. Historically at Zillow a separate generator service produced each of these campaigns, and each service carried its own workflow, data models, and business rules. As the number of notification campaigns grew, so did duplicated engineering work, inconsistent behavior, and operational cost. Product teams needed to launch campaigns faster, reuse shared capabilities, and run consistent experiments without system-specific work. To meet that need, the Zillow Comms Experience team, working with AWS, built two things. The first is the Campaign Orchestrator, which is a configuration-driven orchestration layer that runs each notification as a short-lived workflow execution on Step Functions Express Workflows. The second is the Universal Content Generator (UCG), a library of reusable, schema-driven content modules that those workflows call. Together they make campaign creation faster and more consistent, and they give AI-assisted tooling a declarative format to work with. The challenge: why the original system needed replacing The previous content generation model slowed product delivery. Zillow’s Comms Experience supported more than 20 email and push campaigns generated by more than 10 microservices. Each microservice owned its own workflow, models, business rules, and assembly logic. Most campaigns followed the same pattern: receive a trigger, hydrate data, apply rules, assemble content, and send the message. Each campaign service implemented that pattern separately, creating duplicate engineering work and inconsistent behavior. It also added operational overhead across releases, monitoring, logs, dashboards, and on-call support. Each campaign was built as its own service because, when these systems were first built, scale was the main challenge. As Zillow added more products, the tradeoff changed. Similar features ended up implemented differently across campaigns, so every new capability had to be rebuilt and retested in each service. That made it hard to roll out features across products and slowed development. The push to centralize came from that cost: we needed to move faster and stay consistent across every customer experience. With one shared implementation, a feature could be built once and reused everywhere, while each campaign kept the flexibility to tailor its experience. Before evaluating workflow engines, we first had to extract shared logic into reusable modules and move campaign decisions into configuration. The following diagram shows the original architecture, where each campaign generator carries its own copy of the workflow, data models, and business rules. Figure 1: Original system Competitive evaluation We evaluated Temporal, Flowable, an in-house engine, and Step Functions Standard and Express Workflows against four criteria. Those criteria were reliability, total cost of ownership, development speed, and how well the service would scale across teams. The engine had to be managed, configuration-driven, and able to orchestrate both newer and older services. Pricing also had to fit our volume. Temporal and Flowable would have added another infrastructure component to operate. That worked against two of our core goals: cutting the release, monitoring, and on-call overhead that the original system created, and getting pilot projects running quickly. Neither is available as a managed AWS service, so we would have had to run and scale them ourselves. Step Functions is serverless, so we had no servers or worker fleets to run, and a team could start a pilot without first setting up infrastructure. An in-house engine offered control but required custom lifecycle management, worker pools, queue integration, and monitoring. Step Functions met the core orchestration needs at roughly a quarter of the estimated build effort and a quarter of the ongoing maintenance effort. It was the clear choice for the minimum viable product (MVP). Express mode compared with Standard mode Our planning model assumed high-throughput, low-latency workflows. The MVP plan ramped from 14 million workflows per day to more than 100 million across all campaigns. At full scale that means several thousand executions per second at peak. Each workflow runs for only a few seconds, and a notification has to arrive while it’s still relevant. We evaluated both Step Functions execution modes, and for our use case Express Workflows were the better fit. The following table shows how Standard and Express Workflows compared against our requirements for each key characteristic: Zillow need Standard Workflows Express Workflows High workflow volume Lower default start quota. Higher default start quota. Low latency Optimized for durable, long-running workflows. Optimized for short-running workflows. Execution guarantees Exactly once, which is stronger than needed. At least once, sufficient with idempotent modules. Our workflows are high volume, short-lived, finish well within the five-minute Express limit, and are designed around idempotent module calls. We validated quota, latency, and operational behavior during the traffic ramp-up. The architecture Campaign Orchestrator is a configuration-driven workflow platform. Each message is input data combined with persisted campaign configuration. The configuration is relatively static for each workflow, while the input data stays flexible based on how the configured steps are assembled. A shared orchestration layer reads queued campaign events, groups work where appropriate, and invokes the corresponding Step Functions Express Workflow for each campaign. Campaign metadata describes product constants, ownership, and Zillow environment features. Workflow configuration describes step topology, step-level configuration, mappings, branching, delay behavior, and send behavior. The following JSON shows a simplified workflow input, combining the message payload with the platform, campaign, and configuration metadata that drive the workflow: { "payload": { "trackingId123": { "recipientId": "user123", "homeIds": ["home1", "home2"] } }, "platformMetadata": { "messageType": "email", "source": "savedSearch" }, "campaignMetadata": { "campaignName": "saved_search_alert", "owner": "comms_experience" }, "config": { "modules": ["user_profile", "property_data", "email_transformation"], "experiment": "cta_test" } } The following diagram shows the new architecture, where a single shared orchestration layer and one library of reusable modules serve every campaign. A message moves through the diagram from left to right. The ingress service queues it, and the router applies campaign controls and starts the workflow. Campaign Orchestrator runs the Step Functions steps, each step calls a UCG module, and the delivery service sends the result.
