clean_content: HERE Technologies and AWS: Accelerating NDS.Live with agentic AI | AWS DevOps & Developer Productivity Blog Skip to Main Content AWS DevOps & Developer Productivity Blog HERE Technologies and AWS: Accelerating NDS.Live with agentic AI NDS.Live development at HERE Technologies demands that dozens of interdependent schema definitions stay consistent with every customer requirement, and agentic AI is how we’re meeting that challenge. HERE’s mission is to deliver a unified map for our automotive customers, and central to this mission is the Navigation Data Standard (NDS). NDS is the global industry standard for map data formats. Major manufacturers like BMW and Volkswagen use it so that navigation, Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), and automated driving systems speak the same language. While NDS Classic focused on batch delivery for offline storage, the industry has shifted toward NDS.Live, a streaming-first standard. With NDS.Live, vehicles can pull high-definition map updates in real time through APIs. This transition significantly increases the burden on our Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). Our map data delivery teams must now manage dozens of interdependent schema definitions. Teams must translate every customer requirement into precise engineering tasks with 100 percent architectural consistency. Adding to the challenge, the automotive industry demands rigorous process compliance. Automotive SPICE (ASPICE), the process assessment model used across the industry, requires bidirectional traceability between system requirements, software requirements, and implementation artifacts. When teams create ticket hierarchies manually and inconsistently, demonstrating this traceability during audits becomes costly and labor-intensive. That effort diverts engineering time from product delivery. Currently, product requirements arrive as high-level feature descriptions. Manually decomposing these into a structured Jira hierarchy is time-consuming and inconsistent across teams. That hierarchy runs from Product Requirement to Epic to Story to Task. Critical domain knowledge is often fragmented across repositories or stored only in the minds of senior architects. Specifically, the relationship between HERE’s internal source data models and the output NDS.Live schemas lacks a single source of truth. This context switching leads to structural errors in tickets, creating a quality bottleneck right before release. The solution: An orchestrated multi-agent approach with Kiro To address this, we’re proving the viability of an orchestrated, multi-agent approach built on Kiro. Kiro is a software engineering agent from AWS, available as an IDE, CLI, or web agent. Using Kiro, you can formalize technical requirements and system designs before any code is generated, using its spec-driven development model. Why orchestration? Rather than using a single, general-purpose AI assistant, we chose an orchestration model that mimics a high-performing engineering team. In complex systems, a single agent can suffer from context window saturation, where too much information leads to hallucinations or missed details. We use a Kiro workflow that routes specialized work to purpose-built step agents. Each step runs with exactly the context it needs, and the workflow sequences and parallelizes them rather than relying on one general-purpose agent to coordinate every sub-step. Each step agent is dedicated to one role. Six persona agents analyze each requirement in parallel: an Architect, a Product Owner, a Tech Lead, a Developer, a Quality Assurance (QA) Engineer, and a Data Modeler. Specialist agents then handle each ticket type. Using Kiro powers The core of this system is the Kiro power, a packaged capability that follows the open Agent Plugins format. Agent Plugins is a vendor-neutral specification, so powers built for Kiro also work across other compatible agent clients. With a Kiro power, you can give the AI agent instant expertise in a specific domain by bundling several elements: Agent Skills : Task-specific instructions, scripts, and reference material that define conventions and guidelines, such as coding standards or architectural constraints. Skills load on demand, so the agent sees only the skill name and its activation trigger until a task needs it. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers : Connecting the agent to live data, such as Jira or HERE’s internal technical schema servers. Automation with Kiro CLI Developers work inside the Kiro IDE while writing code. This initiative needed automation that runs without a developer present, so we used the Kiro Command Line Interface (Kiro CLI). By using the CLI, we can integrate the agentic workflow directly into our continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. A system event, like a Jira webhook, can automatically trigger the transition from a product requirement to a structured Jira backlog. No developer needs to manually coordinate every sub-step. Multi-source context injection We ground our agents in our specific domain using multiple methods: Internal MCP servers : These connect Kiro to live internal knowledge graphs, allowing agents to verify if the source data actually exists before committing to a design in NDS.Live. Additionally, they support alignment with internal architecture and system non-functional requirements. Kiro CLI knowledge indexing : This provides the agent with on-demand, token-efficient access to the thousands of pages of NDS.Live documentation. Code Intelligence : The built-in code understanding layer in Kiro indexes our repositories, supporting natural-language queries against the actual source code during ticket creation. Persistent wiki memory A significant challenge in agentic workflows is context loss between sessions. When a developer returns to a task days later, the AI assistant starts from scratch. It must re-learn project nuances, user preferences, and prior decisions. We addressed this by implementing a three-layer memory system inspired by cognitive science: Semantic memory : Stored facts about the domain, including entity definitions, component relationships, and user preferences. The system remembers which Jira fields map to which schema concepts. It also remembers working preferences, such as a developer’s preferred diagram format for architecture documentation. Episodic memory : Records of past sessions, capturing decisions, discoveries, and open items. When a new ticket references a component discussed three weeks ago, the agent recalls the architectural context from that earlier interaction without the developer repeating it. Procedural memory : Learned workflows and task instructions that improve with each execution. When the agent encounters a pattern it has successfully executed before (such as evaluating a milestone against its test plan), it replays that procedure with increasing confidence. This memory lifecycle is fully automated through Kiro hooks. A record-episode hook fires at the end of each meaningful session and distills the interaction into structured knowledge. A recall-memory hook loads relevant prior context at the start of every new interaction. The result: the AI agent compounds expertise over time, much like a new team member who gets better with each sprint. Code Intelligence for architecture-aware tickets Beyond documentation, our agents need to understand the actual implementation. Using the Code Intelligence feature in Kiro, we clone any relevant repository, index its source code, and make it queryable in natural language. Consider a task to “add error handling to the registry service.” The system does not guess at the current patterns. Instead, it queries the indexed code base: “What error handling patterns does this service currently use?” It then writes acceptance criteria that align with the real architecture. This bridging of documentation and source code is critical. Tickets grounded in actual code patterns are accepted by d

title: Introducing queue consumption mode for Apache Kafka in AWS Lambda | AWS Compute Blog
summary: Introducing queue consumption mode for Apache Kafka in AWS Lambda | AWS Compute Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Compute Blog Introducing queue consumption mode for Apache Kafka in AWS Lambda Queue consumption mode for AWS Lambda event source mappings (ESMs) that subscribe to Apache...
clean_content: Introducing queue consumption mode for Apache Kafka in AWS Lambda | AWS Compute Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Compute Blog Introducing queue consumption mode for Apache Kafka in AWS Lambda Queue consumption mode for AWS Lambda event source mappings (ESMs) that subscribe to Apache Kafka is now available. Queue consumption mode is available on the self-managed Apache Kafka ESM. It covers both Kafka clusters you operate yourself and managed Kafka offerings such as Confluent Cloud and other providers that offer Kafka 4.2 or later with Kafka Queue support. With this launch, you can build queue-style event-driven workloads on Kafka that process records with high parallelism that scales concurrency to match your backlog instead of your topic layout. Queue mode achieves this using Kafka Share Groups (KIP-932) , introduced in Kafka 4.0. With share groups, multiple consumers read concurrently from the same partitions, so Lambda can process records from a single partition across many parallel invocations. The result is parallelism that is decoupled from partition count, without head-of-line blocking and without introducing a second messaging system into your architecture. Many Kafka workloads treat each event as an independent unit of work rather than a step in an ordered sequence: generating image and video renditions after upload, offloading slow work from a user-facing API, scoring transactions for fraud, delivering notifications, enriching records for inference, processing bulk files, buffering ahead of a rate-limited dependency, and ingesting telemetry. Correctness for these workloads depends on processing records quickly, not in order. The Kafka consumer group protocol, however, assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, so a topic with 10 partitions supports up to 10 concurrent consumers. Over-partitioning raises that ceiling but increases broker resource usage, slows rebalances, and still leaves head-of-line blocking, where one slow record stalls every record behind it. Previously, teams moved this traffic to a separate queuing system, adding a platform to operate and new producer code. In this post, you learn how queue consumption mode works compared to the existing stream mode, what broker and cluster requirements your Kafka 4.2 cluster must meet, and how to scale from on-demand defaults to provisioned mode for high-throughput workloads. What’s new This launch adds a ConsumptionMode parameter to the Kafka event source mappings in Lambda. It accepts two values: Stream (the default, matching today’s behavior) and Queue, which uses Kafka Share Groups for parallel consumption. The core primitive in both modes is the event poller , a compute resource that fetches records from Kafka and invokes your Lambda function. Queue mode changes the protocol an event poller uses to obtain those records. Because pollers are no longer bound to individual partitions, queue mode supports higher concurrency. A single poller reaches up to 10 concurrent invocations compared to 5 in stream mode, and queue mode scales independently of partition count. We cover the scaling model in detail later in this post. Stream mode: One consumer per partition, ordered processing ConsumptionMode defaults to Stream , so existing ESMs are unaffected by this launch. In Stream mode, event pollers join a Kafka consumer group , and the broker assigns each partition exclusively to one consumer. This guarantees ordered processing within each partition. Queue mode: Multiple consumers per partition, unordered parallel processing Setting ConsumptionMode to Queue directs Lambda to use the Kafka Share Consumer. Event pollers join a share group , where partitions can be assigned to multiple event pollers for parallel processing without guarantees about order. The broker manages a record lifecycle of Available, Acquired, Acknowledged, and Archived. Fetched records are marked Acquired under a visibility timeout called the record lock duration. A successful invocation acknowledges them. A failed invocation releases them back to Available for any poller to acquire. While an invocation is still running, the poller renews the lock without incrementing the delivery attempt count. Choosing between the modes Use Stream mode when per-partition ordering matters: change data capture, event sourcing, or per-entity state machines. Use Queue mode when records are independent, and you want parallelism that is not bounded by partition count. You can run a Queue mode ESM and a Stream mode ESM against the same topic. Each operates independently through its own protocol. Minimum requirements Before you configure an ESM with ConsumptionMode: Queue , confirm that your Kafka cluster and Lambda function meet the following requirements. Cluster requirements Apache Kafka 4.2 or later, with share groups enabled. Four broker settings interact with your ESM configuration: group.share.partition.max.record.locks – The maximum in-flight records per partition. In Queue mode, multiple pollers might acquire records from the same partition concurrently, so the total in-flight count can exceed a single poller’s batch size. Set this value high enough to accommodate your expected concurrency. When the limit is reached, pollers can’t acquire new records from that partition until existing records are acknowledged, or their locks expire. group.share.record.lock.duration.ms – The visibility timeout for acquired records. In most cases, the default of 30 seconds is sufficient. The poller renews the lock during processing. A long-running function does not typically require a duration longer than 30 seconds. group.share.delivery.count.limit – The maximum number of times the broker attempts to deliver a record before archiving it. This works alongside MaximumRetryAttempts to govern retry behavior. group.share.max.size – The maximum consumers allowed in the share group. When provisioned mode is active, keep MinimumPollers ≤ MaximumPollers ≤ group.share.max.size so that Lambda scaling isn’t capped by the broker. In on-demand mode, Lambda internally manages poller counts within broker-safe defaults. Getting started In the Lambda console, choose your function, choose Add trigger , and select Self-managed Apache Kafka . Enter your bootstrap servers and topic name, set Consumption mode to Queue , and configure your virtual private cloud (VPC) subnets and security groups. Optionally set Minimum event pollers and Maximum event pollers to use provisioned mode. For on-demand scaling leave those empty. The following AWS CLI command creates the equivalent Queue mode ESM in on-demand mode: aws lambda create-event-source-mapping --function-name my-function --self-managed-event-source '{"Endpoints":{"KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS":["broker1.example.com:9092","broker2.example.com:9092"]}}' --topics my-queue-topic --batch-size 100 --self-managed-kafka-event-source-config '{"ConsumptionMode": "Queue"}' ConsumptionMode is the only parameter required to enable Queue mode. BatchSize sets the maximum records per batch sent to your function, accepts values from 1–10,000, and defaults to 100. With AWS CloudFormation, the equivalent resource looks as follows: MyKafkaQueueESM: Type: AWS::Lambda::EventSourceMapping Properties: FunctionName: !Ref MyFunction SelfManagedEventSource: Endpoints: KafkaBootstrapServers: - broker1.example.com:9092 - broker2.example.com:9092 Topics: - my-queue-topic BatchSize: 100 SelfManagedKafkaEventSourceConfig: ConsumptionMode: Queue Queue mode is also configurable through the AWS SDKs, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM), and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). For the complete setup walkthrough, see the AWS Lambda Developer Guide . Scaling with on-demand mode Queue mode ESMs use on-demand mode for scaling by default. Lambda evaluates share group consumer lag at one-minute intervals and adds or removes event pollers as needed, completing scaling actions within three minutes. On-demand mode scales to five event pollers per ESM, each support

title: The State of Ruby Static Typing at Shopify
summary: The State of Ruby Static Typing at Shopify - Shopify Skip to Content blog | Developer Tooling The State of Ruby Static Typing at Shopify by Ufuk Kayserilioglu Published on Dec 7, 2020 Shopify changes a lot. We merge around 400 commits to the main branch daily and deploy a new ver...
clean_content: The State of Ruby Static Typing at Shopify - Shopify Skip to Content blog | Developer Tooling The State of Ruby Static Typing at Shopify by Ufuk Kayserilioglu Published on Dec 7, 2020 Shopify changes a lot. We merge around 400 commits to the main branch daily and deploy a new version of our core monolith 40 times a day. The Monolith is also big: 37,000 Ruby files, 622,000 methods, more than 2,000,000 calls. At this scale with a dynamic language, even with the most rigorous review process and over 150,000 automated tests, it’s a challenge to ensure everything works properly. Developers benefit from a short feedback loop to ensure the stability of our monolith for our merchants. Since 2018, our Ruby Infrastructure team has looked at ways to make the development process safer, faster, and more enjoyable for Ruby developers. While Ruby is different from other languages and brings amazing features allowing Shopify to be what it is today, we felt there was a feature from other languages missing: static typing. Shipit! Presents: The State of Ruby Static Typing at Shopify On November 25, 2020, Shipit!, our monthly event series, presented The State of Ruby Static Typing at Shopify. Alexandre Terrasa and I talked about the history of static typing at Shopify and our adoption of Sorbet. We weren't able to answer all the questions during the event, so we've included answers to them below. What are some challenges with adopting Sorbet? What was some code you could not type? So far most of our problems are in modules that use ActiveSupport::Concern (many layers deep, even) and modules that assume they will be included in a certain kind of class, but have no way of making that explicit. For example, a module that assumes it will be included in an ActiveRecord model could be calling before_save to add a hook, but Sorbet would have no idea where before_save is defined. We are also looking to make those kinds of dependencies between modules and include sites explicit in Sorbet. Inclusion requirements is also something we’re trying to fix right now, mostly for our helpers. The problem is explained in the description of this pull-request: https://github.com/sorbet/sorbet/pull/3409 . If a method has an array in argument, do you have to specify it is an array of what type? And if not, how do Sorbet makes the method you call on the array's element exists? It depends on the type of elements inside the array. For simple types like Integer or Foo, you can easily type it as T::Array[Integer] and Sorbet will be able to type check method calls. For more complex types like arrays containing hashes it depends, you may use T::Array[T.untyped] in which case Sorbet won’t be able to check the calls. Using T.untyped you can go as deep and precise you want it to be: T::Array[T::Hash[String, T.untyped]] , T::Array[T::Hash[String, T::Array[T.untyped]]] , T::Array[T::Hash[String, T::Array[Integer]]] and Sorbet will check the calls on what it knows about. Note that as your type becomes more and more complex, maybe you should start thinking about making a class about it so you can just use T::Array[MyNewClass] . How would you compare the benefits of Sorbet to Ruby relative to the benefits of Typescript to Javascript? There are similar benefits, but Ruby is a much more dynamic language than JavaScript and Sorbet is a much younger project than TypeScript. So the coverage of Ruby features and expressiveness of the type system of Sorbet lags behind the same benefits that TypeScript brings to JavaScript.On the other hand, Sorbet annotations are pure Ruby. That means you don’t have to learn a new language and you can keep using your existing editors and tooling to work with it. There is also no compilation of Ruby code with types to plain Ruby, like how you need to compile TypeScript to JavaScript. Finally, Sorbet also has a runtime type-checker and it can verify your types and alert you if they don’t check when your application is running, which is a great additional safety that TypeScript does not have. Could you quickly relate Sorbet with RBS and what is the future of sorbet after Ruby 3.0? Stripe gave an interesting answer to this question: https://sorbet.org/blog/2020/07/30/ruby-3-rbs-sorbet . RBS is about the language to write the signatures, you still need a type checker to check those signatures against your code. We see Sorbet as one of the solution that can use those types, and currently it’s the fastest solution. One limitation of RBS is the lack of inline type annotations, for example there is no syntax to cast a variable to another type. So type checkers have to use additional syntax to make this possible. Even if Sorbet doesn’t support RBS at the moment, it might in the future. And in the case it never happens, remember that it’s easier to go from one type specification to another rather than an untyped codebase to a typed one. So all the efforts are not lost. Does Tapioca support Enums etc? Tapioca is able to generate RBI files for T::Enum definitions coming from gems. It can also generate method definitions for the ActiveRecord enums as DSL generators. In which scenarios would you NOT use Sorbet? I guess the one scenario where using Sorbet would be counterproductive is if there is no team buy-in for adopting Sorbet. If I were on such a team and I couldn’t convince the rest of the team of the utility of it, I would not push to use Sorbet.Other than that, I can only think of a code base that has a LOT of metaprogramming idioms to be a bad target for using Sorbet. You would still get some benefits from even running Sorbet at typed: false but it might not be worth the effort. What editors do you personally use? Any standardization across the organization? We have not standardized on a single editor across the company and we probably will not do so, since we believe in developers’ freedom to use the tools that make them the most productive. However, we also cannot build tooling for all editors, either. So, most of our developer acceleration team builds tooling primarily for VSCode, today. Ufuk personally uses VSCode and Alex uses VIM. Is there a roadmap for RBI -> RBS conversion for when Ruby 3.0 comes out? No official roadmap yet, we’re still experimenting with this on the side of our main project: 100% typed: true files in our monolith. We can already say that some features from RBS will not directly translate to RBI and vice versa. You can see a comparison of both specifications here: https://github.com/Shopify/rbs_parser#whats-supported (might not be completely up-to-date with the latest version of RBS). What are the major challenges you had or are having with Ruby GraphQL libraries? Our team tried to marry the GraphQL typing system and the Sorbet types using RBI generation but we got stuck in some very dynamic usages of GraphQL resolvers, so we paused that work for now. On the other hand, there are teams within Shopify who have been using Sorbet and GraphQL together by changing the way they write GraphQL endpoints. You can read more about the technical details of that from the blog post of one of the Shopify engineers that has worked on that: https://gmalette.dev/posts/graphql-and-sorbet-and-unit-tests/ . What would be the first step in getting started with typing in a Rails project? What are kind of files that should be checked in to a repo? The fastest way to start is to use the steps listed on the Sorbet site to start running with Sorbet. After doing that, you can take a look at using sorbet-rails to generate Rails RBI files for you, or you can look at tapioca to generate gem RBIs. Since you can go gradual it’s totally up to you. Our advice would be to first target all files at typed: false . If you use tapioca, the price is really low and already brings a lot of benefit. Then try to move the files to type: true where it does not create new type errors (you can use spoom for that: https://github.com/Shopify/spoom#change-the-sigil-used-in-files ). When it come

title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary - Engineering at Meta
summary: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary - Engineering at Meta Skip to content By Sai Nagabhairava , Hannes Roth , Na Chen , Peter Prelich , Jonathan Bergeron This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. A privac...
clean_content: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary - Engineering at Meta Skip to content By Sai Nagabhairava , Hannes Roth , Na Chen , Peter Prelich , Jonathan Bergeron This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside the clients of Meta’s data and processing systems. A system integrates with PrivacyLib once, and new privacy capabilities plug in as modules that reuse that integration. PrivacyLib performs billions of checks every second, and changes are simulated and rolled out per module. For internal AI agents, whose data access paths may not be known in advance, tool calls on supported paths carry agent context to PrivacyLib. The propagated context links each access to its session, so modules can observe data use and block operations that are not allowed. At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly. In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding , data lineage , and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib , a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access. PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows. This blog post focuses on PrivacyLib’s role in the final stage of the PAI workflow. Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved. PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. There are two kinds of modules: Enforcing modules can block a data access. For example, Policy Zones enforces purpose limitation . Observing modules only record a data access. For example, Privacy Probes collects the runtime signals used to discover data flows. As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project. PrivacyLib replaces repeated implementations across systems. Engineering Challenges and Approaches of PrivacyLib at Meta’s Scale PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta: More than a hundred libraries used to access data services, from key/value stores to AI features. Thousands of production services with versions of the deployed library. Millions of assets being accessed daily. Billions of checks every second. Operating at this scale creates three engineering challenges: Challenge Approach Coverage: Systems can have multiple client libraries and legacy integrations, accept direct network calls, and offer direct database access to backing stores. All of them need to be handled to ensure requirements hold no matter the access path. We integrate at two levels: typed client libraries, where PrivacyLib has full request context, and lower network boundaries on remaining RPC paths to get full coverage. Each integrated system maps its native APIs to PrivacyLib’s common operations and provides the inputs required by its configured modules. Once those pieces are in place, the same module can be enabled in multiple systems without a separate system-specific integration. Scale: At billions of checks per second, even a small per-check computational cost becomes consequential across the fleet. Every service in the hot path pays that cost. We compile requirements at build time into their simplest evaluable form and answer most checks from caches inside the process, so the common path avoids a network call. Reliability: Privacy logic runs in the hot path of critical systems, owned by teams that release on their own schedules. A change has to be testable in isolation and reversible on its own, because a fleet-wide rollback cannot be the recovery path. Enforcement is deployed as part of the service that owns it, so a change reaches production through that service’s own pipeline instead of a fleet-wide config push. Walkthrough: Protecting Messaging Metadata To illustrate how everything comes together at Meta’s scale, let’s walk through a privacy requirement that needs to be upheld when processing messaging metadata. Users exchange messages through apps like Messenger, which supports end-to-end encryption . As Messenger routes and delivers those messages, subject to applicable law, its backend systems process non-content messaging data (i.e., messaging metadata), such as information about when messages are sent or delivered, to improve product performance, detect abuse, and protect users from harmful conduct. A variety of these backend services use Logger, a client library that runs in the service process, to write this metadata to data warehouse tables. Before writing a record, the PrivacyLib integration inside Logger invokes Policy Zones, an enforcing module, to check whether the metadata may flow to the destination table. This check is broken down into two parts: what inputs need to be available to make a decision, and how the check is actually evaluated at runtime. After examining these two parts, we look at how PrivacyLib scales across systems and how changes roll out without disrupting the services in the path. PrivacyLib runs inside Logger’s client in the messaging backend service. It combines the request context with the generated destination metadata, invokes the modules configured for the write, and returns the enforcement decision to Logger. Annotating Messaging Metadata Every Logger destination table has a LoggerConfig that describes the records written to it. MetadataTraceLoggerConfig defines one such configuration for message-delivery traces and marks it as containing messaging metadata: final class MetadataTraceLoggerConfig extends LoggerConfigBase { use MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait; public function configure( LoggerFieldDefiner $fd, ): LoggerFieldDefiner { $this->annotateWithTableLevelPolicy(); // Field and destination definitions } } A logging destination can have many writers, so the annotation describing its output data belongs to the destination rather than to each service that writes to it. If every service declared the annotation separately, the declarations could disagree, or a new writer could omit it entirel

data-astro-cid-twmmywjp> As organizations increase the size of their cloud footprint and the complexity of their applications, they face challenges securing their infrastructure and services. Security breaches often go undetected for months, giving attackers time to do extensive harm. Once organizations become aware of a breach, they may no longer have access to the logs that comprise a complete history of the attack, because the time span easily exceeds their log retention window. This prevents teams from answering critical questions about the source, vector, and duration of the attack. And even when organizations do have access to logs, it can be challenging to detect patterns in large volumes of log data to gain the insight necessary to contain and remediate the incident. In this post, we’ll show you how you can use Datadog Cloud SIEM Investigator to conduct historical security investigations that enable you to understand the scope and impact of an attack, regardless of how long ago it occurred. We’ll show you how you can: - Visualize logs to investigate an attack - Find patterns and context in related Security Signals - Manage attacks and mitigate risks with Workflow Automation Visualize security logs to understand the scope of an attack Cloud SIEM Investigator enables you to visualize logs that provide the full history of a security incident. Datadog gives you a cost-effective way to store a deep history of logs, and now you can visualize those logs to see the course and impact of a security breach—even if it began long ago. For example, if your organization discovers a data leak, you can use Cloud SIEM Investigator to inspect logs over a long time span, and look back on progressively older logs to identify the first signs of the breach. Filtering the Cloud SIEM Investigator view enables you to isolate relevant records that can help uncover an attacker’s trail. For example, you can filter to highlight suspicious users or accounts, or see which services an attacker interacted with and the results of those interactions—i.e., whether an attacker’s requests to the service were allowed or denied. This can help you understand the methods employed by the attacker. If you see that a user tries but fails to update the metadata on a large number of Amazon EC2 instances, you might suspect that this user is a malicious actor attempting to gain a foothold inside your AWS environment. In the screenshot below, Cloud SIEM Investigator visualizes AWS CloudTrail logs to show that a single IAM user made requests to the Amazon S3 service. The timeline at the bottom of the page shows that the user has interacted with this service over several days, and a significant portion of those requests generated errors. Following the path of the user’s S3 activity, we can see that they were able to list S3 buckets, which provided them with knowledge of the organization’s infrastructure. We can also see that the user tried but failed to access the bucket policy of the customer-data bucket. This might have been an attempt to identify a bucket with lax access controls and could suggest the start of an attack. *:first-child]:bg-white block tablet:p-9 desktop-sm:p-12 rounded-3xl bg-white max-h-[ca

title: Transforming fleet analytics for Novus Hi-Tech through agentic AI | AWS Architecture Blog
summary: Transforming fleet analytics for Novus Hi-Tech through agentic AI | AWS Architecture Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Architecture Blog Transforming fleet analytics for Novus Hi-Tech through agentic AI Fleet analytics sounds straightforward until you have thousands of vehicles strea...
clean_content: Transforming fleet analytics for Novus Hi-Tech through agentic AI | AWS Architecture Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Architecture Blog Transforming fleet analytics for Novus Hi-Tech through agentic AI Fleet analytics sounds straightforward until you have thousands of vehicles streaming dashcam footage, driver alerts, GPS pings, and speed warnings across 10 countries, all at the same time. At that scale, no team can manually triage every drowsiness alert or investigate every over-speeding event before it becomes a real incident. With over 120 enterprise customers relying on their fleet, Novus Hi-Tech needed a system that would act on the data, not only show it. With AI-powered automation, they achieved a 46 percent reduction in road-behavior violations and a 55 percent drop in drowsiness alerts per 1,000 km. In this post, we walk you through how Novus Hi-Tech, in collaboration with the AWS Prototyping and AI Customer Engineering (PACE) team, designed and implemented an agentic AI solution called FleetGPT. We architected the multi-agent system using Strands Agents SDK and AWS managed AI services, turning IoT data into real-time safety interventions through natural language querying, automated investigation, and AI-powered voice calls to drivers. For years, extracting value from fleet telemetry required significant manual effort. When a drowsiness alert triggered, operators had to validate video footage, assess severity across multiple signals, contact the driver, and log the outcome. Existing fixed dashboards showed the same views regardless of what teams actually needed to know. At scale, this model breaks down because one can’t staff enough operators to catch every warning in real time, and manual analysis becomes the bottleneck. The cost of a missed warning could be a preventable accident. Novus Hi-Tech needed a system that understood the difference between what a fleet manager needs to know, what a customer success analyst is looking for, and what a Command Center operator must act on immediately. The bottleneck The friction between question and answer wasn’t uniform. It created different bottlenecks depending on what teams were trying to accomplish. Every warning that reached the Command Center demanded the same judgment calls. Operators cycled through this decision tree hundreds of times per shift. On the other hand, fleet managers didn’t need individual event response, but pattern recognition: which drivers are trending toward accidents, which routes carry disproportionate risk, which fleets are drifting on safety compliance. Both roles shared the same friction: the time between asking a question and getting an answer. Operators spent too long investigating individual events. Fleet managers couldn’t analyze trends fast enough. Neither could move from question to insight without switching tools or waiting on data teams. Solution overview FleetGPT replaces fixed dashboards with a natural language interface for dynamic querying, investigation, and insight generation. It surfaces video evidence, driver history, and policy in single interactions. Beyond analytics, FleetGPT automates real-time safety interventions. When a critical event occurs, such as repeated drowsiness, over-speeding, or an SOS trigger, the system initiates a two-way AI-powered voice call in the driver’s native language, with user approval. It tracks acknowledgment and escalates when necessary. FleetGPT is built with two core capabilities. Analyst: A conversational intelligence layer where operators and fleet managers query the fleet data, retrieve video evidence, and search policy documents through natural language. Intervention engine: An agentic layer that monitors incoming events, evaluates severity, and executes driver interventions with human approval. Analyst: Natural language intelligence Novus Hi-Tech’s data landscape included separate systems for telemetry, video, and policy documents. FleetGPT unifies these through a single data layer accessed by an agentic conversational interface. Data storage and processing layer Data store Role Key design choice Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Structured data Stores structured telemetry data Amazon DynamoDB High velocity event stream from devices Low latency read-write operations with composite keys optimized for agentic query patterns Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases Implement RAG with agentic system Vector embeddings stored in Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector for semantic retrieval Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL manages the structured analytical backbone. It stores per-vehicle daily aggregates covering distance, fuel, safety scores, event counts, and GPS statistics, plus live snapshots of current vehicle status. It’s the primary target for the Text-to-SQL pipeline. A YAML schema file with column aliases, descriptions, and worked examples is injected into every SQL generation prompt. This grounds the large language model (LLM) on the actual schema and reduces hallucination on column names and join paths. Amazon DynamoDB handles the high-velocity warning event stream. The warning event table uses a composite sort key of warning_code + datetime, enabling efficient range queries by warning type and time window without full table scans. A Global Secondary Index on fleet_id supports fleet-scoped queries without touching data from other tenants. A separate device registry table maps vehicle IDs to country metadata which is the source of truth for language routing in audio alerts. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, indexes unstructured documents including SOPs, compliance policies, product documentation which are stored in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) . The embeddings are generated using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 for storage in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector . This gives operators and fleet managers a single interface for both data questions and policy questions, with no context switching. Orchestration: Strands Agents Figure 1: Solution architecture The system uses a multi-agent architecture built with Strands Agents, where each agent has a distinct role and model assignment based on the complexity of its task. At the top sits the Supervisor agent, running on Claude Sonnet 4.6 (for model availability by AWS Region, refer to Region availability by models ), which handles intent decomposition and multi-step reasoning. It decides what kind of question the user is asking and routes it to the right sub-agent. The Supervisor uses a SummarizingConversationManager from Strands Agents, which preserves the last six messages verbatim while summarizing older turns. This keeps context window usage bounded without losing conversational continuity. For structured data queries, the Supervisor delegates to a Text-to-SQL sub-agent (also Claude Sonnet 4.6). This agent follows a plan-and-execute approach: it first classifies the query type (vehicle data, driver behavior, or operational metrics), then extracts key entities and maps them to database tables and columns. From there, it generates a query plan outlining the relevant tables and operations, and finally produces and executes the SQL. If an error occurs, the agent retries with the error message, original plan, and failed query included in the prompt for self-correction. Figure 2: Text-to-SQL sub-agent flow When a query needs computation beyond SQL (correlation analysis, statistical profiling, trend detection), the Supervisor delegates to a Data Processing sub-agent running on Claude Haiku 3.0 (for model availability by AWS Region, refer to Region availability by models ). Rather than pushing complex processing onto the database, this agent generates executable Python, runs it through a Python REPL tool, and returns the shaped results to the orchestrator. Claude Haiku 3.0, a smaller model than Claude Sonnet 4.6, helps keep the inference cost down for this tier of the pipeline. Each agent has a focused tool surface and scoped system prompt, reducing hallucinatio

[&>.iframe-block-wrapper]:desktop-sm:col-span-8" data-astro-cid-twmmywjp> Code profilers offer detailed insight into the efficiency of application code by measuring things like the execution time and resource utilization of a service. Datadog’s always-on, low overhead Continuous Profiler provides snapshots of code performance for a service that are tagged with key metadata (e.g., region , service , release ), so you can easily identify and optimize inefficient code. This enables you to manage compute costs and resolve performance bottlenecks that affect your users’ experience. Datadog’s profiler allows you to capture code profiles continuously for all of your production instances. Now you can compare those profiles in the profile comparison view to see how the performance and structure of your code change over time. This enables you to answer key questions about code-level performance such as: has a new release improved performance or caused a regression? Is your code more performant in one region, host, or pod versus another? Which functions are consuming the most CPU time for today versus last week? The profile comparison view also helps you quantify the changes you’ve made to fix a performance bottleneck, such as optimizing a CPU-intensive method, so you can easily calculate the estimated savings on your production infrastructure costs. Quickly detect code performance regressions in production workloads As your application grows in size and complexity, the probability of introducing regressions in code performance also increases. Continuous Profiler enables you to view your application’s code performance in production at a glance, whether it be through an instantaneous sixty-second profile or an aggregate view of a service’s performance bottlenecks within a specific timeframe. But there may still be critical performance blind spots that would otherwise go unnoticed without complete visibility into application code. With the profile comparison view, you can efficiently troubleshoot the root cause behind performance blind spots at a method level, including regressions such as: an increase in a service’s heap memory size over the past two days spikes in service latency since the last deployment regressions in CPU consumption over the past seven days The profile comparison view automatically highlights changes in production code performance based on a selected profile type (e.g., CPU time, allocations, thread locks, etc.) and a timeframe that you specify. Visibility into these areas of code performance can help you monitor the efficiency of production workloads and detect problematic areas before they become more serious. For example, you can compare a service’s live heap memory between two releases to spot potential memory leaks. The screenshot below shows a method that is contributing eight percent more to the heap live size in the newer deployed version (in purple) compared to the previous one (in blue). If the service live heap memory continues to increase over a sustained period of time then it could indicate that there is a memory leak within the service. However, your job often includes activities performed outside your IDE, such as working with APIs, creating screenshots, or massaging data. Eric wants to show you how the command-line can simplify, improve, or even automate some of these tasks. Eric provides an overview of utilities that gives you more ways to get your work done and get it done faster. Using real-world examples, you'll learn how to type less in the terminal, search your files with ease, manipulate images and JSON files, write code automatically, and more. All without needing to point, click, or swipe! If you are curious about command-line tools or want to learn more about their impressive capabilities, this talk is for you. This presentation focuses on software available for macOS computers, but Linux and Windows users can benefit, as many of the tools mentioned are cross-platform. This presentation is a 45-minute talk with 15 minutes dedicated to Q&A. Couldn't make the presentation? Here as is a link to the view the presentation .  About Eric Fung Since 2010, Eric has worked on many mobile apps and games and spent five years at Shopify as an Android developer before recently transitioning to a data scientist role. At the beginning of his career, he spent a lot of time in Linux and the command-line. Eric caught the public speaking bug a few years ago and is an organizer of GDG Toronto Android. In addition to coding, he enjoys making and eating elaborate desserts. title: AI-driven database investigation using MCP, Agent Skills, and AWS DevOps Agent | AWS Database Blog
summary: AI-driven database investigation using MCP, Agent Skills, and AWS DevOps Agent | AWS Database Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Database Blog AI-driven database investigation using MCP, Agent Skills, and AWS DevOps Agent In our previous post , we built a custom agent for SQL Server d...
clean_content: AI-driven database investigation using MCP, Agent Skills, and AWS DevOps Agent | AWS Database Blog Skip to Main Content AWS Database Blog AI-driven database investigation using MCP, Agent Skills, and AWS DevOps Agent In our previous post , we built a custom agent for SQL Server deadlock and blocking investigation on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server using Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime . That approach gives you full control, from model choice to deployment. With AWS DevOps Agent , you get the same result without building and running the agent yourself. It’s a managed service that triages alarms, groups related events, and sends findings to your team’s channels. Your database administrator (DBA) investigation process is written as a skill instead of a system prompt. AWS DevOps Agent investigates operational events autonomously and delivers findings to your team. In this post, we walk through the architecture that exposes SQL Server diagnostic tools to AWS DevOps Agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. The tools run in an AWS Lambda function, and AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , hosts the MCP endpoint. We also show how an AWS DevOps Agent skill defines your DBA team’s investigation steps, severity thresholds, and report format. The sample’s AWS CloudFormation stack handles the setup. We then follow two investigations that combine built-in Amazon CloudWatch telemetry with direct SQL Server access through the Gateway. Solution overview This solution uses AWS DevOps Agent, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, and AWS Lambda to automate database investigations for Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server. The complete implementation is available on GitHub at sample-agentic-db-ops-sqlserver . The following diagram shows the architecture. Figure 1: Solution architecture connecting AWS DevOps Agent to Amazon RDS for SQL Server diagnostics through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway The solution has three main components. AgentCore Gateway AgentCore Gateway is a fully managed MCP endpoint that sits between AWS DevOps Agent and your database tools. You register your Lambda function as a target and define its tool schemas. The Gateway turns MCP tool calls into Lambda invocations, so you don’t run an MCP server. It also provides built-in observability and auditing. An MCP-compatible client connects to the Gateway URL over Streamable HTTP and, in this solution, authenticates with Signature Version 4 (SigV4). It can then discover and call your tools through standard tools/list and tools/call requests. In this solution, the Gateway provides: SigV4 authentication for every caller. Optional fine-grained access policies. In this solution, AWS DevOps Agent can call only the tools on its allowlist. Database credentials stay away from the agent. The query tools Lambda function retrieves them from AWS Secrets Manager . Logs and metrics for each tool call, including the request, response, and duration. Logs require log delivery to be set up. The same endpoint can serve AWS DevOps Agent, your own agents, and other MCP clients. AWS DevOps Agent AWS DevOps Agent is a managed service that investigates incidents. You connect it to your AWS account and to the tools behind your Gateway. The agent receives alarms, decides what to check, calls the tools it needs, and sends findings to your team. It reads AWS data through a read-only AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role. It gets database detail only through the Gateway. The agent has no database connectivity and no access to database credentials. AWS DevOps Agent also: Follows the investigation method in your skill when it picks tools. You can open an AWS Support case from an investigation, with the full context attached. Runs weekly evaluations and recommends improvements before incidents happen. AWS DevOps Agent Skills The AWS DevOps Agent Skills are self-contained instruction files that give the agent specialized domain knowledge and investigation methods built around your environment and how your team operates. Each skill is a directory of Markdown instructions. The sql-server-investigation skill in this post is organized as: sql-server-investigation/ ├── SKILL.md └── references/ └── tool-reference.md The SKILL.md is the only required file. It holds your DBA team’s investigation method in Markdown: when to use the skill, the step-by-step investigation procedure, the decision paths for different scenarios, and the expected outputs. It’s in plain Markdown format. The frontmatter names the skill and says when to use it, and the body holds the five-step method. The structure looks like this: --- name: sql-server-investigation description: | Incident investigation procedures for Amazon RDS for SQL Server performance issues including blocking and lock contention, plan regression, slow or high-impact queries, and missing indexes. Use this skill when investigating SQL Server database latency, high CPU, blocked sessions, query timeouts, or read/write performance degradation. Triggers on requests like "investigate SQL Server blocking", "RDS SQL Server high CPU", "query timeout RCA", "plan regression", or "why is my SQL Server slow". metadata: version: "1.0.0" --- # SQL Server Investigation Structured troubleshooting methodology for Amazon RDS for SQL Server. title: Taming BEAST: Faster, Safer SSL now on CloudFlare
summary: Taming BEAST: Faster, Safer SSL now on CloudFlare | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content For some time, the vast majority of the web has been vulnerable to the so-called BEAST SSL attack. The attack was first demonstrated in 2011 , and more than 90% of the Internet including large sit...
clean_content: Taming BEAST: Faster, Safer SSL now on CloudFlare | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content For some time, the vast majority of the web has been vulnerable to the so-called BEAST SSL attack. The attack was first demonstrated in 2011 , and more than 90% of the Internet including large sites like Google.com remain vulnerable to their SSL sessions being decrypted. But, as of today, anyone with CloudFlare account with SSL need no longer fear the BEAST. The solution to BEAST is implementing TLS 1.1 and 1.2 as well as prioritizing the RC4 cypher suites. We just rolled out support for these across our network. Along with this, we've looked over the SSL cyphers we support. We've added some additional stronger cyphers, removed some of the weakest cyphers, and prioritized them to optimize both security and SSL performance. Faster & More Secure This is one of those great updates where we can report that security has improved and performance is also faster. In fact, this update makes our overall SSL performance about 30% faster. Sites behind CloudFlare now receive a 90 (A) score from SSLLabs. That's higher than the scores achieved by sites like Google.com and Facebook.com , and the highest score we think we can get without sacrificing performance. If you have SSL enabled, you can test yours yourself . All paid CloudFlare plans include SSL by default. If you don't yet have SSL, upgrade to a paid plan today to make sure all the visitors to your site can surf on a secure, encrypted connection. It's now not only the easiest SSL on the web, but also among the fastest and the safest. title: Maintainer spotlight: Daniel Stenberg - The GitHub Blog
summary: Maintainer spotlight: Daniel Stenberg - The GitHub Blog Devon Zuegel · @devonzuegel June 28, 2019 | Updated May 7, 2021 | 7 minutes Share: With the launch of GitHub Sponsors , open source maintainers and developers can apply to receive funding from the community that depends on t...
clean_content: Maintainer spotlight: Daniel Stenberg - The GitHub Blog Devon Zuegel · @devonzuegel June 28, 2019 | Updated May 7, 2021 | 7 minutes Share: With the launch of GitHub Sponsors , open source maintainers and developers can apply to receive funding from the community that depends on their work. Through sponsorship, open source maintainers have the freedom, financial security, and autonomy to continue the work they’re passionate about to further build and strengthen the open source community. Over the next few weeks, we’re sharing the stories of several open source contributors. Learn about their projects, challenges, and what sponsorship means to them. Daniel has been an open source developer for over 25 years. He’s the founder and lead developer on cURL , one of the most widely used open source components in the world. He currently lives in Sweden with his wife and two kids. When he’s not writing code, Daniel likes to hang out with his family or play floorball. Can you tell us a little about the project(s) you maintain? I maintain several projects, but there’s one I’m well-known for in particular. I founded cURL , a command line tool and library for internet protocol-based data transfers specified with a URL. cURL also has a handful of other trusted maintainers, and we fully conform to the Core Infrastructure Initiative’s open source best practices . I’m proud to say that cURL is one of the most widely used software components in the world with an estimated six billion installs. It’s currently shipped by default in Windows 10 and macOS, and it’s available as a package in popular Linux and BSD distributions. Highly portable, you can build and run it on virtually any operating system. You’ll find it used in mobile phones, TVs, cars, printers, servers, kitchen appliances, and more. Born in 1998, cURL is an old project and has been my primary spare time project and hobby since then. We’ve had more than 650 contributors and we’ve thanked over 1,900 people for their help. After all this time, the development, speed, and activity of the project are still high. Features are constantly added and bugs are fixed as we keep up with internet trends, browser updates, and new technologies—it never ends. Why did you start or become involved in this project? I became involved to satisfy my desire to build and code. In 1996, I worked on an open source IRC bot and I wanted to offer a service to exchange currencies. This meant that I had to download currency rates almost daily—luckily I found a site that hosted rates. Using this information, I wanted to create a simple tool to download an HTTP name was changed to httpget . I quickly became a maintainer and when I added support for Gopher, the name changed to urlget . This was a descriptive name until I added support for FTP, at which point I had to rename it again. It transfers based on a URL, it’s a client, and it allows you to view the contents of a URL—that’s when cURL was born. cURL 4.0 was released on March 20, 1998 with around 2,000 lines of code. It took off and we’re currently at 160,000 lines and growing. What do you think is the biggest challenge that open source faces? The biggest challenge open source faces is maintenance. When different interests pull in different directions, the maintainers need to continue following their roadmap. Companies can often be persuaded to pay for new features and extend open source projects, but it’s not as easy to pay and take the time for project maintenance and fixing bugs. Often we see paid developers working on incorporating a highly visible feature while the long-term work—that requires patience, time, and deep technical and architectural understanding—is taken on by unpaid volunteers in the project. These patterns can end up bad for projects in the long run, since it doesn’t allow the project to be sustainable, let alone successful. Making an open source project is easier than ever. The infrastructure to get a project out to the community is smoother, and making it searchable as well as notifying users has improved tremendously over the years. The sheer amount of projects is exploding, and the total amount of code in the world grows at an amazing speed, both with proprietary and open source. Every project today competes with millions of others for attention from contributors and developers—and users. If there isn’t any demand or need for my project, why should someone invest in it? Why would someone contribute to your project? And how would you get food on the table while spending time to maintain the projects you think are valuable? The match between what companies think are the right priorities to work on against what an individual wants to work on is a constant struggle and challenge for open source developers. Our biggest hurdle to overcome is convincing companies about our recommendations and views, along with gaining an understanding of the commercial aspects and needs of our projects. How has your involvement in this project helped you grow, personally or professionally? This project defines me and my career to a high degree. I’m known for cURL. My career and professional life are focused and revolves around this project. I’ve spent more than 15,000 hours in my spare time working on this project. I now work full-time with cURL support. cURL is my life. I joined the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), and I’ve worked with protocol development and standardization there for over 10 years thanks to cURL. And I get to make contributions to help improve HTTP and the internet as a whole. What is the greatest contribution need for your project now or in the future? We’re a small project, team-wise. We always lack developers to help out in various aspects of the project where our regular maintainers aren’t experts. We’re also an internet transfer project, so we must keep up with how internet transfers are done by browsers, what other major companies are doing, and what users want. We need people involved in the project with an understanding of our history, our current roadmap, and what’s coming in the horizon. Companies and individuals will always contribute new features when they feel a need, but we need people to maintain and polish these additions. We also need contributors to be empowered to say no when necessary, and help newcomers feel a sense of community. cURL is a foundational component of a vast number of internet-related software and devices—we don’t want it to break! Why did you sign up for GitHub Sponsors? I signed up because I want to encourage all efforts that make it easier for open source developers and maintainers to get sponsored for their work—and I think Github Sponsors could work. I signed up to be part of the beta and provided my feedback for (and on behalf of) our community. An awesome sponsorship system could be really good for a lot of people and for open source, and I’m happy to be part of any efforts to make this happen. What do you want potential sponsors to know about you and your project? Sponsoring me helps cURL maintenance. It ensures that the cURL project can keep its trajectory forward and remain independent from larger players. It will ensure continued debugging, packaging, user support, release management, and everything that no one is usually paying anyone to do. Anyone thinking of sponsoring me can learn about who I am, what I’ve accomplished, and my history with the cURL project for the past 21 years. I do open source and internet protocols and standards—and I don’t intend to stop, ever. Sponsors will help me stay true to this. Sponsor Daniel Stenberg Want to learn more about featured maintainers? Read about: Mariatta Wijaya Sean Griffin Henry Zhu Russ Magee Check back soon—we’ll be adding new interviews every week. Contact us If you have ideas about how GitHub Sponsors can better serve the open source community. [&>.iframe-block-wrapper]:desktop-sm:col-span-8" data-astro-cid-twmmywjp> Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) are templates for launching and scaling Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances. Because Amazon EC2 AMIs are reused across environments and automation pipelines, decisions about how you build, source, manage, and share them directly affect your cloud attack surface. You can source AMIs for your EC2 instances in three ways: create and privately share base images (golden images) within your accounts, use public images from a trusted publisher, or use community images from another AWS account. Each option reflects a different trust boundary and introduces distinct risks. In 2025, Datadog’s security researchers identified a scenario where retrieving the newest and potentially unvetted AMIs from a public repository can increase an environment’s exposure to certain types of supply chain attacks. This post looks at how image sourcing and life cycle management can impact your cloud attack surface, along with best practices to mitigate that risk in the following areas: Reduce insecure configurations, vulnerabilities, and version drift in private AMIs Prevent sensitive data leakage when sharing Amazon EC2 AMIs Detect and block untrusted or malicious public AMIs Reduce insecure configurations, vulnerabilities, and version drift in private AMIs Many teams maintain golden images so they can standardize the process for configuring and provisioning instances. However, the trade-off is that decisions around how you manage an image’s patch levels, installed packages, security guardrails, and other configurations need to be replicated with every launched instance. In addition, golden images are often built on top of public or community AMIs, which means any associated risks become embedded in the internal image. For example, if one of these AMIs includes a remotely exploitable weakness, such as a network-accessible service running with weak or default credentials, every instance launched from it inherits the same initial access path. You can mitigate this risk in how you build and update images. For images you build from scratch, the Center for Internet Security (CIS) benchmarks can help you standardize secure defaults. If you create images from other AMIs, treat the base image and any dependencies as part of your supply chain. Your base image checks should include retrieving them from trusted sources and scanning them routinely to catch vulnerable packages before distribution. Strategies for maintaining AMI inventories For handling updates, you have two options: apply patches at instance boot time, or regularly rebuild and publish new AMIs. Applying patches at boot time enables you to keep a stable golden image while ensuring every instance applies security updates during initialization. Rebuilding AMIs regularly gives you the ability to automatically apply any necessary updates and speed up initial boot times. Maintaining an AMI inventory across your accounts and regions helps you apply these recommendations reliably. You can start by answering the following questions: Which private AMIs exist across your accounts and regions? How many instances running in production were launched from each private AMI? title: CloudFlare's Buenos Aires data center now online
summary: CloudFlare's Buenos Aires data center now online | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content Che, ya estamos en Argentina! It is con placer that we announce our 32nd data center in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Our Buenos Aires data center is our 5th in Latin America following deployments i...
clean_content: CloudFlare's Buenos Aires data center now online | Cloudflare Blog Skip to content Che, ya estamos en Argentina! It is con placer that we announce our 32nd data center in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Our Buenos Aires data center is our 5th in Latin America following deployments in Santiago , São Paulo , Medellin , and Lima . As of this moment, CloudFlare is now mere milliseconds away from nearly all of Latin America's 300 million Internet users. Argentina may be better known as the land of bife and malbec, but it is also home to a thriving tech community, including several well known start-up accelerators such as Startup Buenos Aires , Wayra and NXTP Labs (a CloudFlare customer!). At CloudFlare, we know a thing or two about the challenges of building a technology company, and we're proud to support the fast delivery of Internet applications for users in Argentina, as well as those who create them. Don't cry for me Argentina Although not commonly known, the title of the famous song from the musical Evita originates from an epitaph on a plaque honoring Evita Peron , and roughly translates as: "Don't cry for me Argentina, I remain quite near to you." Unfortunately, when it comes to the Internet, there is plenty of reason to cry (or at least sniffle), as the majority of online content consumed within Argentina (and all of Latin America) must be transported from quite far away. Prior to our deployment in Buenos Aires, delivery of the nearly 2 million Internet applications on CloudFlare to the majority of Argentina's 35 million Internet users occurred through CloudFlare's data centers in Newark and Miami (200 and 170ms, respectively, of RTT away from Buenos Aires), with the remainder served in-region from our other data centers in Latin America. In both cases, multiple International carriers are involved in delivering traffic from our network to the ultimate end user. Also keep in mind that this issue is not CloudFlare specific. The vast majority of online content consumed in Latin America is delivered from even further away in the various geographies in which it is hosted (Europe, Asia, Oceania, etc.), with even more severe latency. At play are two overarching, and related, dynamics. The first relates to the domicile of online content. It is estimated that upwards of 80-90% of online content accessed in Latin America is hosted outside of Latin America. This also includes locally produced content, as the cost of hosting is often less expensive in the United States and Europe. Consequently, to access online content Internet users within Latin America must travel longer distances, which means a slower Internet. This is where CloudFlare steps in allowing any individual or enterprise to easily localize their content across our global network. In regions where ISPs/networks are highly interconnected, this typically means that one or more CloudFlare's data centers is very close by. However, in regions with less local interconnection, such as in Argentina (and Latin America at large), the closest point of interconnection may be quite far away (as in the case above with traffic routing to Newark and Miami). This is where the second dynamic comes in: interconnection. For many ISPs in Latin America, it is less expensive to purchase Internet connectivity in the United States (e.g., delivered across a submarine cable), than to purchase that same access locally. As a result, interconnection between ISPs/networks frequently occurs outside of the region, which means that content can only be accessed outside of the region (even if it is hosted locally!). Fortunately, much progress is being made to foster network interconnection locally. This progress takes the form of increased competition between providers on price and quality of service, a policy environment that recognizes the importance of local interconnection, and the development of local IXPs (Internet exchange points). Latency, meet your maker If you're on CloudFlare, your content is, as of today, available locally It is this last development—the formation of IXPs—that is greatly facilitating the local interconnection of networks and the exchange of content. As part of our Buenos Aires deployment we've established connectivity with CABASE , an association of IXPs in Argentina. CABASE's association includes numerous interconnected IXPs throughout Argentina, allowing ISPs from Mendoza to La Plata to exchange traffic within the country. CABASE, like PTT.br (an IXP in Brazil in which CloudFlare is also a participant) is a great model for Internet connectivity in the region. Our participation in the IXP allows us to cache our customers' content locally, and exchange it with ISPs across the entire country. Say hasta luego to Newark and Miami (sorry Will Smith). For those that read our previous post about our Düsseldorf deployment, we encouraged readers to guess our next three datacenter locations. Only one guessed Buenos Aires, but two more locations are at large. Stay tuned!
